headline: Balloons from Lahore college event land on Himachal rooftop, police launch probe
content: A bundle of balloons carrying a banner linked to a women's college in Lahore, Pakistan, was found on the rooftop of a house in Himachal Pradesh's Solan district, prompting police to verify its origin and trace how it travelled into Indian territory. The balloons carried a banner bearing the inscription ‘Annual Sports Day-2026, Govt. Graduate College for (W) Township, Lahore’. They were found on the rooftop of a house belonging to Jai Parkash, a resident of Dhdogi village near Arki. The police seized the balloons and the banner for examination and registered a daily diary report (DDR) at the Arki police station. Solan Superintendent of Police Sai Dattatreya Verma told The Indian Express that preliminary cyber research had established the existence of Government College for Women in Township, Lahore, Pakistan. The police also found videos circulating online showing balloons being released during the college’s Annual Sports Day celebrations on November 19, two days before the bundle was found in Solan. “We came to know that the college exists in Pakistan. Our cyber research also revealed that its Annual Sports Day was held on November 19, when officials released balloons. The investigation is underway,” Verma said. The SP further said that balloons bearing the insignia of Pakistan International Airlines had also been found earlier in Solan. The aerial distance between Lahore and Solan in Himachal is approximately 272 km. Via road, Lahore is approximately 400 km away from Solan. A police officer said, "We found an account on Facebook named Ggcwt Lahore, the acronym for Government Graduate College for Women Township, Lahore. Many posts and videos show that the annual sports day was organised and balloons were released in the college on November 19. A Pakistani politician, Sajida Farooq Tarar of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), was shown as the Chief Guest at the annual sports meet." The latest incident comes amid a series of similar recoveries reported from Himachal Pradesh. Balloons bearing Pakistani markings have previously been seized in Una, Kangra and Chamba districts, raising concerns and prompting police inquiries into their origin and possible route into the state.

headline: Caught growing cannabis? Here’s how the law determines your punishment
content: On November 17, separate police parties raided two farms in villages 12 km apart in Gujarat’s Rajkot district, following tip-offs that cannabis plants were being grown there. Growing cannabis without a licence is illegal in Gujarat, and yet some farmers take the risk. The crop is usually harvested in November and December, keeping the police on alert. The two farmers were booked under different provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. Here's why. The seizures A team from Vinchhiya police station in rural Rajkot raided a farm in Kharachiya Jas village and found seven cannabis plants growing amid cotton on a 2.5-bigha plot belonging to 40-year-old Paba Magan Panchala. The police uprooted the plants and seized 14.45 kg of cannabis valued at Rs 7.225 lakh. They completed the seizure by evening. About 12 km to the west of Kharachiya Jas, the Special Operations Group (SOG) of the Rajkot Rural Police raided a farm in Chhasiya village of Vinchhiya taluka at 3 pm the same day. But the police completed their panchnama only 15 hours later, at dawn on November 18, after weighing the ganja from plants that 55-year-old Savshi Bachu Mithapara had already harvested on his five-bigha plot of land. The total seizure amounted to 705.49 kg, valued at a whopping Rs 3.52 crore. Mithapara, who had harvested the cannabis crop just four days before the police raid, was booked for possession of ganja, an offence that carries a maximum prison term of 20 years for commercial quantities. Panchala, meanwhile, was booked for cultivating cannabis, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years, regardless of the number of plants involved. Why the difference of a decade? The FIRs in both cases were filed at the same Vinchhiya police station. Paba Magan Panchala, whose cannabis plants were still standing during the police raid, was booked under Sections 8(b) and 20(a) of the NDPS Act, which prohibit and penalise the cultivation of any cannabis plant. The maximum punishment is 10 years and a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh, regardless of whether the accused cultivated one plant or an entire field. By contrast, Savshi Bachu Mithapara, who had already harvested his crop, was booked for possession of ganja under Sections 8(c) and 20(b) of the NDPS Act. These provisions cover the production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport and use of cannabis, among other activities. Marijuana, or weed, known as ganja in India, consists of the flowering or fruiting tops of the cannabis plant. Under the NDPS Act, seeds and leaves are excluded from this definition when they are not accompanied by these tops. Since the quantity seized from Mithapara's field exceeded 20 kg, the threshold for a ‘commercial quantity’ of ganja, the punishment prescribed under Section 20(b)(ii)(C) is rigorous imprisonment of at least 10 years, which may extend to 20 years, along with a fine ranging from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 2 lakh. Why the condition of the crop matters There is no difference between the prescribed street value of cannabis plants and ganja decided by the Government of India. According to an October 24, 2025, notification issued by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, all forms of ganja are valued at Rs 50,000 per kg. This is a fivefold increase from the earlier valuation of Rs 10,000 per kg, police officials confirmed. Asked why Mithapara had been booked under the more stringent provisions of the NDPS Act despite having cultivated the crop, Inspector Fatehsingh Pargi of the Rajkot Rural SOG told The Indian Express, "The accused Mithapara had cut down the plants and set them out to dry. The number of plants could not even be counted because they had been completely dismantled branches, root and stem. So, our case is not that of cultivation of cannabis but falls in the definition of possession of ready product known as ganja." Inspector AC Damor of Vinchhiya police station similarly said that Panchala had been booked for cultivation because the police found standing cannabis plants in his field, rather than a harvested product. When is cannabis cultivation legal? The NDPS Act generally prohibits the unauthorised cultivation of cannabis plants as well as the production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport and consumption of narcotic drugs. However, there are exceptions for cannabis, with state-level rules allowing licensed cultivation for scientific or medicinal purposes. Uttarakhand and Madhya Pradesh have legalised cannabis cultivation for several years. Himachal Pradesh joined them in July, permitting the controlled cultivation of cannabis for medicinal and scientific purposes.

headline: Himachal assembly clears Bill to fast-track investments
content: Dharamshala: The Himachal Pradesh Assembly on Saturday passed Himachal Pradesh Investment Promotion and Facilitation Bill, 2026, providing a comprehensive statutory framework to accelerate inclusive, balanced, sustainable and green industrialisation in the state, chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu said in a statement.“The passage of this landmark Bill marks a decisive step towards establishing Himachal Pradesh as a transparent, responsive and competitive investment destination. It will replace procedural complexity with time-bound facilitation, digital approvals and clear institutional accountability. Our govt’s objective is not merely to attract investment, but to secure responsible and sustainable investment that generates quality employment for Himachali youth, strengthens local enterprise and promotes balanced development across the state,” the CM said.Expressing satisfaction over the passage of the Bill, industries minister Harshwardhan Chauhan said, “The passage of this landmark Bill reflects the state govt’s firm commitment to making Himachal Pradesh a transparent, responsive and competitive investment destination. It provides a comprehensive framework for time-bound approvals, digital clearances, investor facilitation, development of land banks and accountable decision-making. The legislation will accelerate balanced and green industrialisation, attract responsible investment and create meaningful employment and entrepreneurship opportunities for the youth of the state.”He added that the legislation would provide a legal framework for Himachal Pradesh’s upcoming industrial policy.A key feature of the Bill is the establishment of a Single Window Approval, Clearance, Reviewing and Monitoring Authority, headed by the chief minister, to ensure time-bound processing, approval and implementation of investment proposals. A dedicated state-level facilitation mechanism will assist investors and coordinate clearances across state and central govt departments.The Bill also provides for a comprehensive digital platform and a Combined Application Form for regulatory and non-regulatory approvals. It introduces self-certification for eligible investors, auto-renewal and perpetual validity of notified approvals, risk-based inspections, easier exit procedures and an automatic appeal mechanism for applications delayed beyond prescribed timelines. It also provides for the involvement of stakeholders in the decision-making process through an Industrial Advisory Forum.The legislation further envisages the creation of a land bank comprising suitable public and private land, optimal utilisation of industrial plots, development of industrial estates, clusters and green corridors, and public-private participation in industrial infrastructure.It also provides for a high-powered mechanism involving the govt, industry and registered transport operators to rationalise logistics and freight rates.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in ChandigarhStay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. headline: Himachal assembly clears Investment Promotion Bill | Hindustan Times
content: The Himachal Pradesh assembly on Saturday passed the Himachal Pradesh Investment Promotion and Facilitation Bill, 2026, during the last day of the winter session, proposing a series of measures to promote investment and industrial development in the state.The Bill, which was earlier introduced by industries minister Harshwardhan Chauhan in the House, seeks to establish a comprehensive statutory framework for investment facilitation, including a time-bound approvals, digital processing of applications, self-certification, auto-renewal of specified approvals and reduction of regulatory compliance requirements.Chauhan said, “We are bringing this legislation because every state has enacted such a law. Through this Act, we are providing a legal framework to the policy so that there is clarity. This legislation is in the interest of the state.”Under the proposed legislation, the government will establish a single window approval, Clearance, Reviewing and Monitoring Authority, headed by the chief minister, with the industries minister as its vice-chairperson. The chief secretary and secretaries of industries, revenue, power, finance, and environment, science and technology will be its members.The authority will be responsible for ensuring time-bound processing, approval and implementation of investment proposals. It may also constitute project review and approval committees at the state and regional levels to examine proposals and expedite clearances.The Bill also proposes setting up a dedicated Investment Promotion and Facilitation Cell in the industries department to assist investors in obtaining approvals and coordinating with various state and central government departments.On the passage of the bill, chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu, said, “The passage of this landmark Bill marks a decisive step towards establishing Himachal Pradesh as a transparent, responsive and competitive investment destination. It will replace procedural complexity with time-bound facilitation, digital approvals and clear institutional accountability.”The legislation provides for the creation of a land bank comprising public and private land parcels. The government may acquire land in accordance with the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, and make government land available for industrial clusters, estates, common facilitation centres and related infrastructure.Jan Vishwas Bill gets nodThe House also passed five other bills on the last day of the winter session. It includes the Himachal Pradesh Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill 2026, which seeks to promote trust-based governance by decriminalising minor offences and rationalising penalties for procedural lapses, technical defaults and other minor contraventions under various state enactments. It aims to reduce the compliance burden on citizens and business establishments, minimise litigation and ease the burden on the judicial system.

headline: 'Criticise decisions, not constitutional institutions': CJI Surya Kant
content: <p>Shimla: Chief Justice of India Justice <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/surya-kant">Surya Kant</a> on Sunday said that citizens in a democracy have the right to criticise the decisions of constitutional bodies but should avoid targeting the institutions themselves.</p>.<p>Interacting with students on the sidelines of the 10th convocation of the Central University of Himachal Pradesh (CUHP) at Dharamshala, where he was the chief guest, the Chief Justice observed that people often fail to distinguish between a decision and the institution behind it.</p>.<p>According to him, this tendency risks undermining public confidence in institutions essential to sustaining democracy, a university statement said.</p>.<p>While citizens in a democracy have the right to criticise the decisions of constitutional bodies, they should avoid targeting the institutions themselves, he said.</p>.SCBA seeks contempt action against lawyer for sharp personal remarks against CJI Surya Kant.<p>In his convocation address on Sunday, Justice Surya Kant drew on the Himalayan landscape around him to urge the graduating students to be patient in pursuing their goals, reminding them that the road to any destination in the mountains is seldom straight and that no one climbs a mountain alone.</p>.<p>The convocation was held at the auditorium of Government Degree College, Dharamshala. Degrees were conferred on 702 students and 32 gold medals were presented, 23 of them to women.</p>.<p>The 702 graduates included 584 postgraduates, 29 undergraduates and 48 PhD scholars, besides diploma holders. The university newsletter and five books by faculty members were released on the occasion.</p>.<p>Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu told the students that a degree is not only recognition of a student's hard work but also represents their responsibility towards society and the nation.</p>.<p>Emphasising that any country's greatest strength lies in its educated, aware and responsible citizens, he said education is not merely about securing employment; it is a means of developing critical thinking, understanding, research, innovation and bringing positive changes to society.</p>.<p>In an era of rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, data science and digital technology, the education system must prepare young people not only to seek employment but also to generate employment, undertake research and promote innovation, he was quoted as saying in the statement.</p>.50 years of 42nd Amendment to Constitution: How 'secular and 'socialist' survived.<p>Governor Kavinder Gupta called upon the university to work towards emerging as a centre of impactful research on Himalayan challenges, including climate change, disaster management, water conservation, biodiversity and rural development, stressing that universities must connect academic excellence with the needs of society.</p>.<p>"Knowledge empowers us, values give us direction and determination enables us to achieve our goals. Your degree may earn you recognition, but your character and values will earn you lasting respect," he said, urging students to remain committed to integrity, humility and lifelong learning.</p>.<p>Highlighting the ecological and cultural significance of the Himalayas, the Governor said development must be pursued in harmony with nature.</p>.<p>He urged the university to promote focused research on Himalayan ecology, disaster preparedness, water resources, tribal communities, natural farming and tourism, so that academic pursuits contribute to sustainable development in the region.</p>.<p>Chief Justice of the Himachal Pradesh High Court, Justice Gurmeet Singh Sandhawalia, and Deputy Chief Minister Mukesh Agnihotri were among those who attended the ceremony.</p>.<p>The Vice Chancellor of the university, Sat Prakash Bansal, said the university's vision was 'local to global'.</p>.<p>He highlighted its debut in the 701-800 band of the Times Higher Education World University Rankings and its 239th place in Southern Asia in the QS Asia University Rankings, and said its h-index had risen from 22 to 86 and its patents from one to 70.</p>

headline: India’s smallest State leads the way on roads
content: Author: Vikant SahayIn India most discussions about roads focus on big expressways, metro systems and traffic in large cities. Many a times the most important lessons come from smaller states. Take states like Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Tripura, Sikkim, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh. These places face challenges of hilly terrains and less of flat land. They depend a lot on two-wheelers as their roads are often narrow or winding and dealing with sudden spikes in over-excited tourists especially during seasons.From March 2019 onwards how these smaller states handled rising vehicle numbers tells a story. It shows what governance, strong institutions and focus on safety can do.As pandemic lockdowns ended in May 2020, road accidents across India began to rise. Data from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways shows that in 2022 there were over 4.6 lakh road accidents and by 2024 that number had gone up to 4.88 lakh. Deaths on roads crossed the figure of 1.77 lakh. Many smaller hill states and northeastern states found it hard to keep up.Steep slopes, slow emergency services and dangerous highway spots made crashes more deadly. In 2024 the national average was 36 deaths for every 100 reported crashes and in the State like Uttarakhand had more than 62, Meghalaya had over 73 and Mizoram had than 93.Then there is the smallest State in the country, Goa. It stood out as between 2023 and 2025 road accidents in the State fell steadily and the number dropped from 2,846 to 2,370, which is a 17 per cent drop. While most states were seeing increases Goa was going down.More impressive is how serious the crashes were. In 2024 Goa had 286 deaths in 2,682 reported accidents. That means under 11 deaths per 100 crashes which is less than a third of the average.What makes Goa different from its neighbours and other smaller States in India? It did not rely on temporary police crackdowns and instead, it made changes. Over the years it transformed road management through technology, better engineering and stronger public transit.A key step was replacing manual systems with digital ones. Most small states still struggle with services but Goa built a strong digital backbone. It moved core services like vehicle registration, driver licensing and permits onto platforms and it linked 49 transport services to Aadhaar authentication. This made permit issuance fully digital and for this step it earned national praise too.At border checkposts like Mollem, Pollem and Patradevi in Goa automated vehicle checks started. Urban intersections were monitored with cameras. Over five years Goa issued 2.6 million electronic challans which is more than Uttarakhand, a larger hill state. Interestingly, it is more than triple the number in Tripura.One big win was freight monitoring on the roads. From 2020 to 2024, Goa had zero accidents and zero deaths caused by vehicles. In other states overloading caused dozens of deaths every year.In the two years, Goa pushed forward with new policies and physical upgrades. It introduced the Goa Road Safety Policy 2025. This policy uses intelligence and data analytics to manage traffic. It includes a safety audit of 5,500 km of roads and it targets engineering fixes at 43 high-risk accident spots.Goa also launched a vehicle scrapping facility. It has already dismantled 1,280 government and private vehicles. This is supported by tax breaks and full waivers on fines.In April 2026, the Directorate of Transport of Goa moved into a modern office in Porvorim and it now has a command and control center. Plans are underway to install automated number plate recognition cameras at 91 locations across the state.What really sets Goa apart is how it combines strict rules with clean accessible public transport. It did not leave people stuck with cars or unregulated operators, instead, it modernized the Kadamba Transport Corporation Limited.By 2026 electric air-conditioned buses made up about a quarter of the Kadamba fleet. Plans are in place to add 100 electric buses to the fleet. Smart transit cards are being launched and these offer fare discounts for regular commuters.At the anniversary of the Kadamba Transport Corporation in Panjim on October 2 last year Chief Minister Dr. Pramod Sawant said something important. He called Kadamba buses Goa’s lifeline. He credited the public transport network for helping economic growth and added that the state is moving fast toward full digitisation. The Mhaji Bus Yojana supports private stage carriage operators. This shows Goa treats transport as a basic service. Not something to ignore or delay.The lesson for small states across India is simple. Geography and size should not stop progress. Data from the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances shows Goa has a 68 per cent digital service portal reach that is four to five times higher than states like Tripura, Sikkim and Meghalaya. While many northeastern states are still planning their automated testing centers and scrapping plants Goa has already made those part of daily life.As India works to cut road deaths in half and move towards transport infrastructure, many look to big industrial states for models and the past seven years show something else. Small states can move faster and better when leadership and reform go hand in hand.Goa’s journey since 2019 proves that safe roads, efficient services and reliable electric buses are not just, for cities. With vision and steady action even India’s smallest state can lead the way.Vikant Sahay has 30+ years of experience in journalism, diplomacy, and public policy. He served as Sr Political Advisor to the US Consulate General in Kolkata & Sr Advisor to Lieutenant Governor of Delhi; Views presented are personal.

headline: Himachal Pradesh Government
content: · Chief Minister attends 10th convocation ceremony of Himachal Pradesh Central University; Congratulates Students Chief Justice of the Himachal Pradesh High Court, Justice G.S. Sandhawalia, congratulated graduating students at Himachal Pradesh Central University's 10th convocation in Dharamshala. Chief Minister Thakur Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu while extending best wishes to the students receiving degrees at the 10th convocation ceremony of Himachal Pradesh Central University, held in Dharamshala today, said that a convocation ceremony is not merely a milestone in an academic journey but also marks the beginning of a new chapter in life. It celebrates years of hard work, discipline, perseverance and the fulfilment of dreams, with parents and teachers playing an important role in this achievement. The Chief Minister said that a degree is not only recognition of a student's hard work but also represents their responsibility towards society and the nation. Education is not merely about securing employment; it is a means of developing critical thinking, understanding, research, innovation and bringing positive changes to society. He emphasized that the greatest strength of any country lies in its educated, aware and responsible citizens. He said that in an era of rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, data science and digital technology, the education system must prepare young people not only to seek employment but also to generate employment, undertake research and promote innovation. The Chief Minister stated that the State Government considers education a vital foundation for development and self-reliance. The government's objective is to provide the youth of Himachal Pradesh modern knowledge and technology and enable them to establish their identity at national and international levels. Considering the challenging geographical conditions of the state, he said that it is the government's responsibility to ensure access to quality education and resources for children living in remote villages.

headline: Retired employees win ₹33.95 lakh gratuity battle as Supreme Court says pending appeal cannot delay retirement benefits
content: Two retired Delhi Development Authority (DDA) employees can receive their pending gratuity of nearly ₹34 lakh, after the Supreme Court ruled that their retirement benefits cannot be withheld indefinitely because the government has challenged their acquittal in a corruption case. The court said retired employees should not be made to wait for years for their terminal benefits when the trial court's acquittal order remains in force and there is no stay on it.In its November 16 judgment in Delhi Development Authority vs Rajender Kumar Sharma and another, the Supreme Court dismissed two appeals filed by DDA against orders directing it to release the employees' gratuity with applicable interest. The relief is subject to the employees giving an undertaking to refund the amount, along with interest, if the pending judicial proceedings eventually go against them.Why did DDA withhold the gratuity?The two employees, Rajender Kumar Sharma and Satendra Pal, joined DDA in 1984. Sharma initially worked as a lower division clerk, while Pal joined as an assistant field investigator. Both were subsequently promoted and retired from service in 2021 and 2018, respectively.Their gratuity was withheld because of a corruption case dating back to 2001. The Anti-Corruption Branch of the Delhi government had registered an FIR against several officials, including the two employees, alleging that they had included fictitious names in a survey of slum dwellers eligible for relocation and alternative plots, allegedly in connivance with property dealers.In February 2017, a special court convicted four co-accused but acquitted Sharma, Pal and seven others. The state subsequently approached the Delhi High Court, seeking permission to appeal against their acquittal. The High Court issued notice in August 2017, but the challenge remained pending.DDA withheld gratuity of ₹18,52,224 payable to Sharma and ₹15,43,113 payable to Pal, citing Rule 69(1)(c) of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972. The provision bars payment of gratuity until the conclusion of departmental or judicial proceedings and the issuance of final orders.What did the Supreme Court say?The employees approached the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in 2023 after DDA rejected their representations seeking release of gratuity. In January 2026, the tribunal directed DDA to release the amounts with applicable interest, subject to an undertaking by the employees to refund the money with interest if the judicial proceedings ultimately went against them.The Delhi High Court upheld the tribunal's decision in March 2026. DDA subsequently challenged the orders before the Supreme Court.The Supreme Court held that the mere pendency of the state's application seeking permission to appeal against the acquittal could not justify withholding the employees' terminal benefits, particularly when no stay had been granted against the trial court's judgment.The bench also distinguished the case from its decision in Bikram Chand Rana vs Himachal Pradesh Road Transport Corporation (2026), which dealt with an employee whose criminal trial was still pending. In the present case, the trial had concluded with an acquittal, making the gratuity payable.The court observed that an appellate court could overturn the acquittal, but until that happened, the acquittal continued to hold the field.Why did the court allow gratuity with a refund condition?The Supreme Court said the undertaking to refund the money was intended to balance two competing interests: protecting public funds and ensuring that retired employees could access benefits earned over decades of service.It noted that requiring retired employees to wait indefinitely for appellate proceedings against their acquittal to conclude could make their pensionary benefits practically meaningless.The bench said employees should not suffer because of prolonged proceedings initiated by the state, particularly when the delay was not attributable to them.It also held that the refund undertaking adequately protected DDA's financial interests. The court found no reason to interfere with the tribunal and High Court orders and dismissed both appeals.

headline: Day 6: Sukhu announces inquiry into cases of beneficiaries being wrongly declared dead in records
content: Kullu: Himachal Pradesh chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu on Saturday announced an inquiry into cases of beneficiaries being wrongly declared dead in official records, resulting in the discontinuation of their assistance under the Mukhya Mantri Sahara scheme.The CM also announced that eligible people left out of the scheme could submit their names to the concerned department for verification, with govt committing to cover all eligible beneficiaries by December 20.Sukhu made the announcements during the Question Hour on the concluding day of the Winter session while responding to allegations by the Leader of Opposition that living beneficiaries, including people who were bedridden and severely disabled, had been declared dead in govt records and consequently deprived of financial assistance under the Sahara scheme.Responding, the CM said that any case in which a person had been wrongly declared dead and removed from the scheme would be investigated.Appealing to all members of the House to identify people who had been left out, Sukhu asked them to submit their names to the concerned department. Govt officials would verify their eligibility, he said.Earlier, the Leader of Opposition alleged that a large number of people registered under the Sahara scheme had been declared dead despite being alive. Citing a case from his Seraj constituency, he said a family had brought a severely disabled young man to meet him in a vehicle because he could not move his arms and legs following a spinal cord injury.The woman accompanying him told him that she had visited the govt office to enquire about the discontinuation of the assistance and was informed that the official records showed her husband to be dead, the opposition leader said.Describing the incident as one among several such cases, he accused govt of lacking sensitivity towards people dependent on the scheme.Meanwhile, before adjourning the assembly, Speaker Kuldeep Singh Pathania informed that the House held six sittings between November 16 and 21, conducting business for approximately 24 hours with 80% productivity.Pathania said govt replied to 366 questions, including 242 starred and 124 unstarred questions. The House also passed 13 govt bills after discussion, said Speaker.Box:Himachal Pradesh Assembly on Saturday passed six bills, including new legislation aimed at providing a legal framework for industrial development and investment promotion in the state.The Himachal Pradesh Investment, Promotion and Facilitation Bill, 2026, was passed after a debate in which BJP MLA Vikram Singh questioned the need for a fresh law when the state already had an industrial policy and the Himachal Pradesh Single Window (Investment Promotion and Facilitation) Act, 2018.Replying to the objections, Industries minister Harshwardhan Chauhan said the 2018 Single Window Act, enacted during the previous BJP govt, had not been implemented and had subsequently become null and void.The new legislation provides for digital and online processing of clearances and NOCs using the latest technology, he said.The other five bills passed by the House were the Shimla Road Users and Pedestrians (Public Safety and Convenience) Third Amendment Bill; the Himachal Pradesh Khadi and Village Industries Board (Amendment) Bill; the Himachal Pradesh Public Trust (Amendment of Provisions) Bill; the Himachal Pradesh Municipalities (Amendment) Bill, 2026; and the Himachal Pradesh Municipal Corporations (Amendment) Bill, 2026.

headline: A Dham Good Feast
content: A steaming mound of unpolished local rice is ladled onto a fresh leaf plate. A barefoot cook, dressed in a traditional dhoti and kurta, moves with practised ease along the rows of seated guests, carrying a copper bucket. Leaning forward, he ladles out the next course: Aloo Chana Madra, a slow-simmered, yoghurt-rich delicacy enriched with khoya. Across Himachal Pradesh, every region, from Mandi to Chamba, has its own interpretation of dham, the traditional ceremonial midday feast. This particular spread, served in the shadow of the Dhauladhar range, is Kangri dham. There are no pre-plated thalis here. A full dham comprises nine to 11 vegetarian dishes, each served individually and in a prescribed sequence, allowing its distinct flavours to unfold.“A traditional dham consists of rice and several lentil preparations. There are no chapatis,” says Sanjay Mishra, the master Boti (hereditary chefs entrusted with preparing dham), whom everyone reverentially addresses as Panditji. The 51-year-old, who hails from Pathiar village in Kangra, has spent more than three decades preserving this culinary tradition. “We use freshly ground local spices and mustard oil, with every dish prepared separately. Our traditional cooks still wear dhotis, go barefoot and serve the food using buckets and ladles,” he says, as he watches over the hearths with quiet authority..Course follows course at an unhurried pace. There is Sepu Badi, made from three ground lentils; split chickpea dal perfumed with fennel seeds and dry coconut; and Teliya Mah, a dark urad dal cooked in mustard oil, its subtle, smoky aroma filling the air. As the meal progresses, the flavours move from rich and savoury to sweet and tangy. The savoury sequence culminates in Kale Chane Ka Khatta, a dark, tangy black chickpea gravy with pumpkin and radish. Its distinctive, almost inky colour comes from walnuts roasted until charred and then ground with dried mango into a fine powder. The dish prepares the palate for the final course: Meethe Chawal, sweet rice glistening with khoya and dried fruits. “Once people sit down, nobody gets up until the sweet rice is served,” explains Mishra.Dham was an integral part of Chef Nitika Kuthiala’s growing-up years. The Noida-based culinary researcher and writer, who hails from Kangra, is also behind the food pop-up Pahadi Pattal. She recalls how the traditional meal marked occasions ranging from mundan ceremonies to weddings. “Most dham meals are rice-based, saatvik and eaten during the day, although some regions may include a few non-vegetarian preparations. The menu changes from place to place,” she says..The Botis begin cooking in the early hours of the morning. Before preparations commence, the floor of the open-air kitchen is cleansed with a mixture of cow dung and clay. “Until the food is prepared and offered as bhog to the divine, the Botis do not taste a single morsel,” Mishra explains. With no onions, garlic or commercial spice blends in the kitchen, the cooks rely on local ingredients and inherited techniques.For Chetna Chopra, Culinary Director at OMO, dham offers a window into the social and cultural fabric of Himachal. “It’s particularly moving that the process begins not with an ingredient or a recipe, but with an act of reverence towards the fire itself.” Seated together on the ground, with no distinction of status, guests partake of a meal that is as much about community as it is about food. In the unhurried rhythm of its service, the careful preparation of each dish and the reverence that underpins the entire ritual, Himachali dham offers a compelling lesson in slow food, collective belonging and the grace of sharing a meal..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: Bill to promote investment passed amid heated debate in Himachal Assembly
content: The Legislative Assembly on Saturday passed the Himachal Pradesh Investment Promotion and Facilitation Bill, 2026, by a voice vote amid a heated debate over the absence of a specific provision ensuring 80 per cent employment for Himachali youths in industries.Industries Minister Harshwardhan Chauhan and Jaswan-Pragpur MLA Bikram Thakur sparred over the need for a new legislation when the state already had the Industrial Policy, 2019, and the Himachal Pradesh Single Window Investment Promotion and Facilitation Act, 2018.Bikram Thakur questioned the government why it had brought a new Act when most of its provisions were already covered under the existing industrial policy. He also sought to know why the 2018 Act had not been implemented and whether it had been amended or incorporated in the new legislation.He said that the proposed Bill was silent on the provision in the 2019 Industrial Policy mandating 80 per cent employment for Himachali youths in industries. He sought an assurance from the government that this provision would be incorporated in the new framework.Chauhan said that an industrial policy need to be flexible and could be interpreted differently, whereas an Act provided a clear legal framework and greater certainty for investors as well as the government. He cited similar industrial development legislation in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh to justify the need for a separate law.Chauhan said that the 2018 Act, passed during the previous BJP government, had never been implemented as its commencement date was not notified. The new legislation would provide for online and automated clearances and streamline the process of obtaining no-objection certificates from various departments, he added.On the 80 per cent employment provision, Chauhan assured the House that it would be incorporated in the rules to be framed under the new Act. He said that the rules would provide detailed safeguards to ensure industries complied with the requirement and strengthen the state’s ability to act against violations.The minister urged the members to support the Bill, saying a dedicated legal framework was necessary to promote industrial investment and protect the interests of the state. The Assembly passed five other Bills, namely The Shimla Road Users and Pedestrians (Public Safety and Convenience) Third Amendment Bill; The HP Khadi and Village Industries Board (Amendment) Bill; The HP Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill; The HP Municipal (Amendment) Bill and; and The HP Municipal Corporation (Amendment) Bill.

headline: Mired in controversy, Karnataka's environment bodies get more mining powers
content: Bengaluru: At a time when environment authorities at state level are riddled with allegations of incompetence and corruption, the Centre has increased their powers to give clearance to mining projects. Under the Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006, development projects, ranging from mining and industries to apartments and dams, are divided into Category A (large) and Category B (relatively smaller) projects. These are scrutinised and cleared by the Central and State governments, respectively. At the state level, the notification set up State Environment Impact Assessment Authorities (SEIAAs) and State Environment Appraisal Committees (SEACs) to appraise and clear projects involving a built-up area of 20,000 square metres, non-coal mining projects covering 50 hectares, power projects of up to 50 MW, among others. Mining projects In the case of non-coal mining, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC) amended the notification to enhance the powers of SEIAAs and SEACs, increasing the size of projects they could appraise and clear by 10 times in less than five years. While the original limit of 50 hectares was increased to 250 hectares in April 2022, the Ministry, in a notification dated November 18, has now raised it to 500 hectares, an area equivalent to 700 football pitches. Gaps in governance Last year, DH reported on a letter from the Principal Accountant General raising objections to the State's violation of rules in the appointment of the technical director of the SEAC, despite objections raised by officials in the Environment Department. .'No one likes Hyderabadi biryani here': SP's Azam Khan takes jibe at Owaisi over alliance, slams 'environment of hatred' in UP.The only basis for the appointment, the letter noted, was "telephonic instructions" from the chief minister. In at least two instances, the SEIAA and SEAC were also found to have approved projects based on erroneous EIA reports containing content copy-pasted from older projects. The SEIAA has also faced allegations of corruption in the granting of quarry permits in Ramanagar. Sandur-based activist Sreeshaila Aladahalli said the Centre's move to notify the relaxation would further compromise the EIA appraisal system. "There is a reason why the original EIA notification had allowed state authorities to clear only projects up to 50 hectares. In the years since, the importance of environmental regulations has only gone up. Considering the misgovernance in the state authorities, there is no rationale for this notification," he added. Dodda Aswhathanarayana Swamy, who moved the Karnataka High Court against the Centre's move to allow persons with master's degrees in arts and business to become members of the state authority, said the notification would allow "open loot" of resources. "This is not decentralisation, it is an open route to loot. Handing massive mining appraisals to SEACs without fixing their competence or accountability removes vital central oversight from broken panels. Across India, qualified experts are sidelined," he added.

headline: What Chief Ministers' Home Portfolios Mean for Governance
content: In India, public perception over safety, crime prevention, communal harmony, narcotics control and security matter a lot and they have become increasingly complex governance challenges. Hence, the Home Department remains one of the most consequential portfolios in a state government. That is why from largest state Uttar Pradesh’s Chief Minister (CM) Yogi Adityanath to the Smallest State’s CM Dr Pramod Sawant, hold the Home Portfolio. Other states where CMs retain the Home portfolio include Maharashtra, Assam, West Bengal, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Punjab. They have take up this responsibility of a direct control of policing as it strengthens coordination and decision making. However, the real measure lies in transparent performance, institutional independence, public safety and overall public perception on their governance and accountability.Several Chief Ministers have chosen to retain Home, believing that direct supervision allows quicker decision-making, stronger coordination, and clearer accountability. Among them are prominent leaders such as Yogi Adityanath in Uttar Pradesh, Devendra Fadnavis in Maharashtra, Himanta Biswa Sarma in Assam, Suvendu Adhikari in West Bengal, Mohan Yadav in Madhya Pradesh, Bhajan Lal Sharma in Rajasthan, Pushkar Singh Dhami in Uttarakhand, Bhagwant Mann in Punjab and Dr Pramod Sawant in Goa.The Home Department is considered sensitive as it oversees the police, law-and-order arrangements, security infrastructure, intelligence coordination, prison administration and other related institutions. A Chief Minister holding Home can directly review police performance, intervene in administrative bottlenecks, coordinate with district authorities and respond to crises without depending on another minister's political or administrative priorities.But centralisation has its limitations. The Home Department is an enormous operational system, with thousands of police personnel, multiple district units, specialised agencies, intelligence networks, forensic institutions and a large volume of routine administrative decisions. A Chief Minister simultaneously handling finance, personnel, development, party management and political affairs may not have sufficient time for continuous oversight of policing. The effectiveness of the arrangement therefore depends less on the portfolio's political ownership and more on the quality of the professional machinery, delegation, monitoring systems and institutional discipline.Chief Ministers such as Yogi Adityanath, Devendra Fadnavis and Himanta Biswa Sarma have retained Home as part of their broader governance approach. Their states face distinctly different challenges. Uttar Pradesh must manage a vast population, complex law-and-order demands and urban-rural policing. Maharashtra's challenges include metropolitan crime, organised criminal networks, industrial security, and the administration of a large police force. Assam has additional concerns involving border security, insurgency-related issues, migration. and regional security.Similarly, the Home portfolio in smaller states can be particularly demanding despite a comparatively smaller population. Geography, tourism, border exposure, social diversity, urbanisation and the nature of economic activity can create specialised security requirements. In Goa, the challenges include maintaining public safety in a major tourist destination, narcotics trafficking, coastal security, cybercrime, traffic management, foreigner-related violations, and the protection of a fragile social and environmental ecosystem.Goa offers an interesting case study in the Chief Minister retaining the Home portfolio. CM Dr Pramod Sawant, not only holds the Home Department, but several other key departments. His governance approach has increasingly involved coordination with central agencies, modernisation of policing, technology-driven administration and a focus on strengthening institutional response. For a small state with a high tourist inflow and significant coastal exposure, maintaining law and order is closely linked with its economic reputation. The safety of tourists, residents, businesses and investors directly affects Goa's tourism-led economy.The state has also been working on the implementation of the new criminal laws and the Interoperable Criminal Justice System (ICJS), which seeks to improve coordination between police, courts, prisons, forensic laboratories and other institutions. During a September 2026 review meeting chaired by Union Home Minister Amit Shah alongside Sawant, state officials reported an increase in the conviction rate from 22 per cent to 53 per cent and said several criminal cases were being disposed of within six to eight months. The review also highlighted coastal security, cybercrime, narcotics-related offences, and the movement of criminals across state boundaries as priority areas.This improvement, if sustained and measured consistently, could indicate progress in investigation, prosecution coordination, and the use of technology. Goa Police's response time under the emergency helpline 112 was also reported to have improved from 18 minutes to eight minutes. Goa Police's President's Colour (September 2026), the State's first rank in the BPR&D's February 2026 assessment of the three new criminal laws, and Bicholim Police Station's fifth national rank in 2025 offer concrete markers of progress. Initiatives such as Spot the Scam, the Radical Content Analyser and the Pink Force also illustrate technology-led, citizen-focused policing.Reacting to allegations of increasing gang violence and zero fear of the police in the state by Goa Congress, CM Pramod Sawant accuses opposition parties and the INDIA bloc of attempting to create anarchy and unrest in the country. Emphasising his zero-tolerance approach on violence and "goondagiri," he says, “I have given a complete power to Goa Police to act firmly in the interest of law and order, and I urge everyone to respect their authority and cooperate with our police personnel in maintaining peace and security across the State.”In Goa, the CM’s approach towards institutional autonomy and professional policing is particularly valuable. The state's compact geography offers the advantage of relatively close coordination, but its tourism-driven economy, coastal vulnerabilities, seasonal population fluctuations, and emerging cyber and drug-related threats require constant preparedness. Stronger intelligence-sharing, community policing, modern surveillance with safeguards, forensic capacity, coastal coordination and victim-sensitive policing must be part of a comprehensive security strategy.It is evident that the Home portfolio is a huge responsibility to protect citizens and uphold the rule of law. Chief Ministers who retain it have an opportunity to demonstrate that concentrated political leadership can deliver efficient, responsive and accountable policing. Goa presents a success story and for the state the next phase must focus on independently verifiable outcomes, stronger investigations, prevention of narcotics and cybercrime, transparent police accountability and greater public confidence. Finally, public perception is the key. Citizens should feel safer, justice is delivered faster, policing is impartial and institutions become stronger. Political control may centralise authority, but only institutional performance can legitimise it.The writer is a senior journalist and columnist with over three decades of experience. He writes extensively on rural affairs, agriculture, economic issues, healthcare and public policy, with a particular focus on developments impacting the grassroots economy and rural communities; Views presented are personal.

headline: How Goa reimagined last mile governance
content: Author: Avijit DwivediOver the last several decades, the standard story of public administration in India has been a rather depressing one. Huge sums of money are announced for various welfare schemes, funds are even allocated on paper, but the schemes fail to reach the intended beneficiaries in remote villages of the country. Many such schemes are also mired in red-tapism. In October 2020, when the Chief Minister of Goa, Dr Pramod Sawant, conceived of Swayampurna Goa, the country was still grappling with the economic shockwaves of the pandemic. In the state of Goa, the economy is largely dependent on the tourism and mining sectors. The Chief Minister realized that the state could not continue to depend on external factors for its economic recovery and that it was high time for the state to look inwards and build self-reliance on the basis of its human and natural resources, starting from the village level through the panchayats.Inspired by Atmanirbhar Bharat, the architecture of Swayampurna Goa was built by Chief Minister Dr Pramod Sawant keeping in mind the geography of the small state of Goa and its decentralized system of Panchayati Raj institutions. This scheme was aimed at ensuring that the residents of Goa did not have to run after the administration in taluka headquarters for getting their rightful entitlements. Rather, the administration would reach out to the residents of villages in the state and deliver services at their doorstep by sitting with the sarpanch of the village in the courtyard of the village.Unique Scheme for Goa: The Scheme is unique in terms of its operationalization and a cadre of Swayampurna Mitras (field officers) has been created for each village panchayat in the state. More than 200 senior gazetted officers from various departments in the State have been allocated a village panchayat / municipal ward each.These officers, who are otherwise confined to their offices, have to leave their offices every Saturday to visit the allotted village and work with local elected representatives, self help groups, teachers and youth clubs to conduct door to door surveys of the village to find out the gaps in the implementation of various welfare schemes and also to address the grievances of the villagers on the spot. A web based portal is being used to monitor the progress of various activities on a weekly basis and the Chief Minister of Goa is reviewing the progress of various activities on a regular basis through virtual interactions with the Swayampurna Mitras and also with the beneficiaries.The unique governance model of Goa has gone through several phases in the last six years. In the first phase of the Scheme, the main focus was on the saturation of various basic welfare schemes to provide water, electricity, pensions, health insurance and housing to all eligible households. The Scheme has now moved to the second phase, namely, Swayampurna Goa 2.0, with the main focus being on economic generation, skill mapping and promoting rural entrepreneurship.Goa will grow local, make local, buy local and sell local to ensure farmer prosperity said the Chief Minister of Goa, Dr. Pramod Sawant on August 17, 2026 at a seedling distribution program held at Panjim. Swayampurna Goa, a initiative of Chief Minister Dr. Pramod Sawant, is in its 6th year of implementation and the Chief Minister launched Seva Sankalp Abhiyan on October 2, 2026 to celebrate the 6 years of the initiative.In addition to the aforementioned agrarian programs, the state of Goa has celebrated six years of the Swayampurna Goa initiative through the Seva Sankalp Abhiyan program in October 2026. The state is now exploring the use of artificial intelligence to further streamline citizen service delivery.The administrative scale of Goa is unique. There are only 191 village panchayats and 13 municipalities in Goa. Hence, Goa can be used as a living laboratory for implementing various administrative reforms to make governance more effective and efficient. In larger states, there are several layers of administrative intermediaries at the district level. These are abolished in Goa and the desk bound bureaucrats are converted into weekly field officers. Thus, instead of looking at a village from the narrow perspective of his/her department, an engineer, agricultural officer or revenue official is forced to look at the village holistically.The results achieved by the Scheme Swayampurna Goa have also generated tremendous interest in other parts of the country. Goa has achieved full coverage of household tap water under the Jal Jeevan Mission, near total saturation of social security pensions and substantial mobilization of women-led self-help groups for setting up micro-enterprises. These achievements were showcased by Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his interaction with Swayampurna Mitras and beneficiaries from Goa recently. A delegation from Assam visited Goa recently to study the weekly deployment of officers and real-time monitoring of various Schemes through web portals.Lessons from Swayampurna Goa can be drawn by other states of the country. Firstly, administrative reform can be initiated without spending large amounts of money. What is required is to use the available human resource within the system and set the targets and monitor the progress. Secondly, self-reliance can be achieved only by moving away from charity to livelihoods. This means that local producers should be able to sell their produce to local hotels, institutions and urban consumers. Thirdly, technology can be very effective in bringing about transparency but it cannot replace human empathy. In Goa, while the digital dashboards provided transparency, it was the physical presence of the civil servant in the panchayat hall listening to the problems of the elderly villagers that restored people’s faith in the government.The author is an expert in rural advocacy; Views presented are personal.

headline: Tata Sons board meeting this week to revisit listing issue amid row
content: India’s Tata Group is entering a critical fortnight as the conglomerate’s controlling shareholders and holding company has back-to-back meetings amid a governance dispute that has spilled beyond the boardroom. The board of Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, or SDTT—one of the two main charities led by Noel Tata—on Friday approved five philanthropic proposals worth ₹2,000 crore but didn’t discuss the listing of Tata Sons Pvt. Ltd., according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified as the details are not public. The meeting was being keenly watched as it was the first formal gathering since a Tata Sons board meeting in September that exposed an unusual rift between the founding family and directors over a potential listing and Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran’s tenure. Next week, the holding company’s board is expected to revisit these issues. At the heart of the disagreement is whether Tata Sons should pursue a public listing after the Reserve Bank of India designated it an “upper layer” non-banking financial company, a classification that carries a listing requirement. The debate has increasingly come to encompass broader questions about who controls Tata Sons and governance at the Tata Trusts, the philanthropic body which owns 66% in the company. Trustees Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh have separately challenged Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata on governance matters, while local media reports said Jimmy Tata, Noel Tata’s half brother, backed Chandrasekaran’s reappointment and a Tata Sons listing—positions that differ from Noel Tata’s efforts to keep the holding company private. The other key charity, Sir Ratan Tata Trust, is facing regulatory curbs on holding meetings, leaving only SDTT to weigh in on the listing debate. But with the SDTT board leaving out this contentious issue from discussions on Friday, Tata Sons board meeting on 26 November now becomes the focal point to see how this power tussle pans out. Tata Sons oversees companies that generated about $185 billion in revenue in the year ended March and own businesses ranging from Jaguar Land Rover to Tetley tea. A spokesperson for the Tata Trusts didn’t immediately respond to a request for comments on the board meeting discussions. Representatives for Tata Sons also didn’t respond to an emailed query. The dispute burst into public view on 17 September, when Tata Sons directors overruled opposition from Noel Tata on moving ahead with listing-related efforts and extending Chandrasekaran’s term by five years. The disagreements have since spilled into the Tata Trusts themselves. With New Delhi urging an amicable truce but offering no formal mediation, the standoff is already paralysing parts of the business empire central to India’s semiconductor ambitions. The Maharashtra Charity Commissioner’s freeze on proceedings at one of the Tata Trusts has complicated Tata Sons’ ability to hold its annual general meeting, approve audited financials, pay dividends and raise fresh capital. The pressure on the Tata Group intensified this month after the RBI reiterated that Tata Sons must comply with all rules applicable to top-tier NBFCs. The RBI’s 16 November communication came in response to the company’s request for guidance on regulatory compliance. While the letter didn't set a fresh deadline or announce enforcement action, it underscored the limited options available to Noel Tata, who wants Tata Sons to remain privately held. While a public float would subject the holding company to heightened market scrutiny, Noel Tata and some in Tata Trusts fear it will dilute their control and leave the group vulnerable to hostile takeovers. Directors who support a listing have argued that complying with regulatory requirements would remove a persistent overhang and improve governance standards. At the upcoming meeting, Tata Sons directors are expected to review quarterly group performance before turning to the contentious items, according to people familiar with the matter. Noel is expected to press alternatives that could allow Tata Sons to remain privately held, the people said, adding that the agenda, however, is likely to be finalised closer to the meeting as there are several moving parts. Restructuring Proposal One proposal would involve folding Tata Electronics and Tata Consulting Engineers into Tata Sons. The restructuring would convert the company from a pure holding entity into a holding-operating company, potentially helping it avoid the central bank’s listing requirement, although the plan would still need board approval and a no-objection certificate from the regulator. A second proposal backed by Noel Tata supports a plan by minority shareholder Shapoorji Pallonji Group to monetise part of its stake in Tata Sons through a phased capital reduction process. Under the proposal, Sterling Investments Corp. and Cyrus Investments would sell shares in two tranches over 18 months, likely easing some of the pressures that have intensified the listing debate. With Srinivasan and Singh closing ranks, Noel’s hand has also been weakened by the exit of Darius Khambata, who emerged as one of the most vocal defenders of the anti-listing camp and the Tata Trusts’ control over Tata Sons. Khambata, in a recent letter to Srinivasan and Singh seen by Bloomberg News, criticised them for their public campaign against the Tata Trusts’ leadership, questioned their abrupt shift in support for a listing and accused them of taking internal disagreements to regulators and the media. The confrontation has spread beyond the boardroom, with Noel Tata questioning some of Tata Group’s biggest investments as well as the board’s decisions in public. “My worry is that a listing, which is what some people are proposing, will change the Tata way,” he said at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi earlier this month. With 30,000 to 40,000 shareholders, “profit may take precedence over philanthropy”.

headline: JD-U to celebrate Good Governance Day on November 24, honour Nitish Kumar’s work | India News
content: Janata Dal (United) (JD-U) working president and Rajya Sabha member Sanjay Kumar Jha on Sunday said, “Bihar got real freedom from the various ills on November 24, 2005, when Nitish Kumar became the chief minister of Bihar and started a new chapter of overall development in the state.”Jha said Nitish Kumar gave people the real taste of freedom through his good governance. “The country got freedom in 1947, but Bihar’s freedom from poverty and lack of infrastructure, be it roads, bridges, power or schools, happened after Nitish Kumar became the CM on November 24, 2005,” he said.To mark Nitish Kumar’s role as chief minister and honour his contributions to Bihar, the JD-U plans to celebrate Good Governance Day across the state on November 24. Preparations for the celebrations are in full swing, Jha said. “November 24, 2005, marks a significant turning point in Bihar’s history. On this day, under Nitish Kumar’s leadership, Bihar emerged from a period of lawlessness and decline and began a new journey toward development, trust, and good governance,” said Jha. “It will encapsulate Bihar’s journey of change, development, and a new identity, which gave the state a new direction under Nitish Kumar, whose invaluable contribution through a string of development initiatives and the shaping of a modern Bihar is undisputed,” he added.On Leader of Opposition Tejashwi Prasad Yadav’s attack that the Centre had provided no financial assistance for Nitish Setu and that the Prime Minister had come only to inaugurate it for the second time, Jha said the RJD leader should speak about his party’s contributions during the 15 years it was in power.“Why could they never feel the need for a bridge in 15 years? The bridge is a brainchild of Nitish Kumar. He conceived the idea and made it possible at a time when even visualising a bridge of this magnitude was a big thing. Today, the bridge is a reality. Nitish Kumar remained the CM for two decades. This is Nitish Kumar’s work. He is known for a chain of roads and bridges in Bihar. What the situation was prior to him is no secret,” he added.Jha said the RJD should not try to dictate what the name should be. “It is the prerogative of the government. The name ‘Nitish Setu’ has touched the hearts of all Biharis, as his work has touched the lives of all, irrespective of caste and creed. He got the most difficult state to handle and transformed it with his governance style and right intent, and Good Governance Day will cherish that legacy,” he added.

headline: Why India’s Public Policy schools need to rethink how they teach
content: India is witnessing an unprecedented boom in public policy education, with 56 policy schools and universities now offering programmes across the country (Phadnis et al., 2025). Having addressed the challenge of scale, the next question is whether these institutions are equipping students with the knowledge, judgement, and decision-making skills required for the realities of public policy practice. The most important task before India’s public policy schools is to rethink how policy is taught. Producing professionals capable of solving complex governance problems requires more than classroom instructions. It requires sustained engagement with real decisions and trade-offs before graduates are compelled to deal with them in real time, where the stakes are high and mistakes can have lasting consequences.

headline: Sebi WTM Murty asks AIFs, VCs to focus on ethics and governance
content: MUMBAI: Alternative investment funds (AIFs) and venture capital funds (VCs) must get more actively involved in the ethics and governance aspects of a company rather than just focusing on valuations and seeking a timely exit, Sebi wholetime member KVR Murty said on Friday. Murty said AIFs need not chase valuations, as value gets created when ethics and governance are followed from day one. “I am a strong believer in the principle that good governance and ethics create value over the long term. AIFs and VCs appear to be more focused on the valuation part of it from day one and looking to make an exit at the appropriate time. Probably they need to do some more introspection on that,” he added. Murty emphasised that while corporate ownership and management represent distinct roles, they must remain aligned in their accountability to the institution. Murty noted that owners provide capital and bear economic risk, whereas management brings professional expertise and exercises authority. .Referring to the 1999 Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee, he reiterated that shareholders, the board and management are the three constituents of corporate governance, with the board serving as the vital bridge between ownership and management.Murty stated the true test of fairness lies not in how a company treats controlling shareholders or institutions that can influence decisions, but in how it protects the equitable interests of retail investors and stakeholders who cannot.He said disclosures must go beyond merely satisfying a technical format and that investors deserve timely answers to three questions: what has the company done, why has it done so, and what could it mean for the business?.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: AP local body poll results proved public trust in govt: CM Naidu
content: VIJAYAWADA: Observing that the local body election results proved that people always support the government that works for them, Chief Minister and TDP supremo N Chandrababu Naidu stated that the people had endorsed the Government’s commitment to welfare, development and good governance, pointing out that the NDA alliance had received greater support in the local body elections than in the 2024 general elections.The Chief Minister said people across both urban and rural areas had wholeheartedly supported alliance candidates. He described the victory as public recognition of the Government’s two-and-half-years in office.Addressing media persons at his Camp Office in Undavalli on Saturday, the Chief Minister said the people’s verdict had favoured the alliance, whether through EVMs, ballot papers or postal ballots.The alliance had achieved a 96.42 per cent strike rate in Zilla Parishad elections and won 93.15 per cent of the Mandal Parishad seats. It had also registered a 94 per cent strike rate in municipal elections. He pointed out that the YSRCP’s vote share had declined from 39.81 per cent in the 2024 elections to 33.56 per cent in the current local body elections.The Chief Minister said his vision was to reduce the influence of money in politics and encourage leadership based on public service. Recalling an incident in which a voter reportedly deposited money offered by a candidate into the ballot box along with the ballot paper, he said it reflected growing political awareness among the people. .He said it was a positive development for democracy when voters recognised the value of their votes and refused to be influenced by money. Public service, performance and credibility should matter more than money in politics, he added.He said adequate representation had been provided to BCs, SCs, STs, women and weaker sections in proportion to their population.Of the 22 Zilla Parishad chairperson posts the TDP won in the elections, 12 had been allocated to women, including 14 graduates and postgraduates among those selected, he said.Of the 20 Zilla Parishad Vice-Chairperson posts, 11 had been allotted to women, with 17 of the selected candidates being highly educated. By entrusting leadership responsibilities to educated youth, the Government was laying the foundation for effective administration in local bodies, he added.The Chief Minister said the government would also analyse the results in certain areas, including Alluri Sitarama Raju district, and identify the reasons behind the electoral outcome.The Government had made every effort to develop the region, he said, while alleging that some people were being lured through forced religious conversions.The Chief Minister said the performance of elected representatives was also being assessed and that issues involving local leadership would be addressed. He cautioned that some MLAs needed to correct their approach..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: Millets reap a fair deal
content: PERAMBALUR: For years, millets disappeared from Perambalur’s fields as farmers turned to maize and cotton in search of better returns. Now, a farmers’ group is sowing the seeds of a revival by ensuring that those who grow traditional millets also reap larger gains. By guaranteeing a market and paying more than the prevailing rates for organically cultivated millets, the group has brought around 250 farmers across 20 villages back to traditional crops, covering 426 acres and producing nearly 206 metric tonnes over the years.The initiative, led by K Saravanan (45) of Veppur, operates through the ‘Nammalvar Iyarkkai Siruthaniya Uzhavar Urpathiyaalar Kuzhu’, a Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO).Perambalur was once known for cultivating traditional varieties such as kodo millet, pearl millet, barnyard millet, foxtail millet, ragi and sorghum. However, the lack of remunerative prices and proper marketing facilities gradually pushed farmers towards commercial crops such as maize and cotton. Though these initially offered better returns, farmers have increasingly struggled with pest attacks, rising input costs and fluctuating market prices. It was against this backdrop that Saravanan decided to work towards restoring traditional millet cultivation in the district.His involvement began in 2013, when he joined the Barefoot Academy of Governance, an NGO working to empower communities and strengthen democratic governance. The organisation had been invited by the Tamil Nadu State Planning Commission to study backwardness-affected blocks in the state. .During a four-month study in Veppur block, it interacted with farmers, women and other stakeholders before submitting its findings to the government. Saravanan subsequently decided to focus on agricultural issues, particularly the decline in millet cultivation.In 2015, the organisation conducted a seminar to promote organic millet cultivation. Around 200 farmers attended, of whom 20 expressed interest in taking it up. Saravanan assured them that their produce would be purchased at prices higher than the prevailing market rates. He also proposed documenting cultivation expenses, from sowing to harvesting, to arrive at a fair procurement price.The initiative began with seven farmers cultivating kodo millet and black sorghum organically on 5.5 acres. They harvested around 1,350 kg of produce, which Saravanan procured at Rs 30/kg, Rs 5 more than the prevailing market price of Rs 25. With the NGO’s support, procurement continued and the number of participating farmers gradually increased.In 2020, Saravanan decided to take the initiative forward independently and established the FPO in Veppur. He serves as its coordinator, while the organisation currently has 19 members.According to Saravanan, the FPO now procures organically cultivated millets at prices around Rs 7/kg to Rs 9/kg higher than the prevailing market rates. During 2025-26, when the market price was Rs 22/kg, it purchased the produce at Rs 31/kg, giving farmers an additional Rs 9 for every kilogram sold. To strengthen the procurement and processing chain, the group established a millet processing unit at Nannai village in 2021 for Rs 18 lakh, with support from the State Balanced Growth Fund of the State Planning Commission. The unit processes the procured millets into millet rice and other products. The FPO sells millet rice to organic stores at Rs 100/kg, seeds to farmers at Rs 50/kg and whole grains to mills at Rs 36/kg..So far, around 250 farmers from 20 villages have cultivated millets on 426 acres through the initiative, resulting in the production of nearly 206 metric tonnes. The group has also sold around eight tonnes of traditional millet seeds across Perambalur, Ariyalur, Cuddalore, Tiruchy and Villupuram districts through seed festivals and awareness programmes. Explaining the procurement model, Saravanan said the initiative was driven by the objective of supporting farmers rather than making profits.“We initially purchased millets from farmers with the support of the NGO. Now, we use the FPO’s corpus fund and loans available through government support to procure produce every year. Once the produce is sold, we repay the loans and continue the process. The amount left after meeting expenses such as building rent, administrative costs and employee salaries is very little. Our objective is not to make profits but to support farmers and revive millet cultivation for a sustainable future,” he said.The FPO also involves farmers in deciding procurement prices. “We document all the expenses incurred by farmers, from sowing to harvesting, and use these details to decide the procurement price. We visit their fields and purchase the produce directly. We also bear the transportation costs instead of deducting them from farmers’ payments, which are made immediately. Before fixing the price, we hold meetings with farmers and arrive at a decision together. We do not restrict procurement to registered members. We purchase from all farmers who follow organic cultivation practices,” he added..P Banumathi, secretary of the FPO, said farmers had increasingly depended on chemical pesticides and fertilisers for maize and cotton cultivation, raising input costs and exposing them to health risks due to inadequate awareness of safe pesticide use.Though the TN government announced a millet mission in 2022 to promote cultivation, Banumathi said stronger price support and procurement facilities were necessary to encourage more farmers to return to traditional crops.For farmers who have joined the initiative, the assurance of a market has made a difference. “Earlier, farmers were hesitant to cultivate millets as there was no assurance of a market or a fair price for their produce. The FPO’s initiative has given us the confidence to take up traditional millet cultivation again. We can sell our produce directly without worrying about middlemen or transportation expenses,” said V Chitra, a farmer from Anganur village.(Edited by Dinesh Jefferson E).Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest
