headline: He chose cows over foreign shores, at 22, builds a Rs 40-lakh dairy business
content: At a time when many young people in Punjab are looking abroad for better opportunities, 22-year-old Jashanpreet Singh Sidhu has chosen a different path. A graduate from Dhan Singh Khana village in Bathinda district, he has decided to build his future not on foreign shores but on his family’s dairy farm. What began as a childhood routine of helping his father in the fields and tending to a small herd of cattle has, in five years, grown into a business worth around Rs 40 lakh, with monthly milk sales of approximately Rs 2.80 lakh. Jashanpreet was just 17, and still in school, when he decided to turn the family’s modest dairy activity, then largely meant for household consumption, into a commercial venture. The family owned five to six cattle, but they were not of the quality required for commercial dairy farming. He gradually acquired knowledge of the trade, sold three of the existing animals and invested in better-quality Holstein Friesian (HF) cows. Today, he runs a 25-cow dairy farm, built around high-yielding animals, improved management practices and a regular milk-supply arrangement with Verka. His decision was driven as much by his father's influence as by the economics of conventional agriculture. Davinder Singh, who has been farming for years, encouraged him to explore an independent venture. “From working alongside my father while studying to managing a dairy operation, his encouragement remains my biggest inspiration,” Jashanpreet says. The family owns four acres and had earlier cultivated another 100 acres on lease. However, as input costs and rental expenses mounted, Jashanpreet began questioning the returns from conventional farming. The family has since reduced its leased landholding to 30 acres while gradually expanding the dairy business. “We used to take a lot of land on rent. But when I started calculating the returns, I realised that a good-quality cow could generate more income than one acre under wheat and paddy. Why should we keep taking land on rent when leased agricultural land costs around Rs 75,000 to Rs 92,000 per acre, and dairy farming could offer better returns?” he says. Building the business, however, required more than investing in better cattle. Jashanpreet learnt the basics of animal care, including administering injections and providing primary treatment, through practical training and experience. Veterinary assistance is sought whenever necessary, while milking machinery has helped streamline daily operations. The farm follows an open-shed system, with the cows not tied up. Milk production varies from 10-20 litres a day in some animals to 30-40 litres in the higher-yielding ones, with the herd averaging around 21 litres per animal daily. Around half the cattle are in milk at any given time, helping ensure a regular supply. The family currently sells more than 2.5 quintals of milk daily to Verka at Rs 37 per kg. The arrangement, Jashanpreet says, provides the assurance of regular procurement, with milk collected directly from the farm, besides access to the cooperative's wider marketing network and dairy infrastructure. Like many young people in Punjab, Jashanpreet too had once considered moving abroad. His elder sister is settled in the UK, where she had gone for studies, and he had thought of following a similar route. “I also wanted to go to the UK. I thought I would earn by working there on an hourly basis, according to someone else's requirements. But here, in my own business, I can work as much as I want and take it forward according to my capacity. I also do not have to leave Punjab and my parents,” he says. His wife, 21-year-old Arashdeep Kaur, who has completed Class XII, had also aspired to go abroad. The couple married with their own plans and ambitions but have now decided to channel their energies into building the dairy business together. Their next ambition is to move beyond selling raw milk. They have begun preparing ghee and khoya on demand, particularly during winter, and plan to gradually expand their range of dairy products. Jashanpreet says they do not add sugar to their products and hope to establish a market for fresh, quality dairy products under the name Sidhu Dairy Farm. He estimates that 50-60 per cent of the income goes towards farm expenditure, including animal maintenance and other operational costs. The business currently has no outstanding debt. For now, the ambition is to expand the herd to several hundred quality animals and build a stronger market for value-added dairy products. For a young man who once contemplated earning abroad, the idea of success has taken a different shape — one that allows him to stay close to his family while building an enterprise of his own in Punjab.

headline: 9 of family killed as vehicle carrying pilgrims rams into truck in Rajasthan’s Kota
content: Nine people were killed and eight injured as a speeding Cruiser rammed into a truck parked along the roadside near Shambhupura on the Kota-Udaipur National Highway early on Sunday, police said.The victims were members of an extended family, police said, adding that they were returning after offering prayers at the Khatu Shyamji temple in Sikar district.Kota Superintendent of Police Tejeshwani Gautam, along with other officials, reached the spot and oversaw efforts to extricate people trapped inside the vehicle.Preliminary reports suggested that the Cruiser driver may have dozed off at the wheel.The Cruiser was carrying 16 members of an extended family hailing from Maharashtra's Dhule district.Haroon, the truck driver, told reporters that he had parked the truck on the side of the road to check a fault and was standing a short distance away when the speeding Cruiser crashed into the truck.He said he was thrown about 20 feet away from the road, regained consciousness after 10 minutes, called the police and ambulance himself, and sustained injuries to his knees and head.The injured have been admitted to the New Medical College Hospital.The deceased were identified as Usha (60), Sushila (65), Kailash (45), Janvi (6), Sajjan (60), Anita, Babual (60), Janvi (13) and Madhvi (45).The injured included the drivers of both vehicles.

headline: Two minors injured in clash between rival party workers in Patiala
content: In an alleged incident of political violence during the ongoing Patiala Municipal Corporation re-elections, two minor children, aged four and six, were injured in an alleged knife attack in Ward No. 1 (Bharat Nagar). The children are relatives of a close supporter of the BJP candidate from the ward. The attack was allegedly carried out by individuals associated with the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP).As the supporters attacked each other, the children sustained serious injuries and were undergoing treatment at Government Rajindra Medical College and Hospital, where, their condition was stable. One of the children sustained injuries on neck while the other was hit with a cricket bat.The injured workers claimed they were attacked twice and a complaint was lodged with the local police, which had rounded up the two accused. On Saturday morning, they again attacked them. However, AAP has denied the attack and said the alleged brawl was a result of personal enmity.The Punjab BJP Mahila Morcha president Jai Inder Kaur visited the hospital, met the injured children and their family, and assured them of all possible support. The police said they have received a complaint and action will be taken.

headline: Amid National Conference rifts, how Farooq Abdullah has moved to keep flock together
content: Amid discontent among its legislators, the ruling National Conference (NC) in Jammu and Kashmir has initiated an exercise to set up informal advisory / consultative groups comprising three-four MLAs to be attached to each minister in the Omar Abdullah-led government for consultations on various measures of different ministries for development and public welfare. The NC leadership has launched this move in a bid to address the concerns of a slew of party MLAs who felt ignored by the recent Cabinet expansion undertaken by CM Omar. Several disgruntled MLAs had met party president Dr Farooq Abdullah and Omar on November 6 to express their grievances. The letters proposing the formation of such advisory groups have been sent by Farooq to all NC MLAs, party sources said. Some of the MLAs also confirmed having received the letters from the NC chief, saying they have been asked to give in writing their choice of three ministers/ministries they would like to be associated with. This would enable the NC high command to finalise the names for all advisory groups. Each of them can be a member of two such groups, some party MLAs told The Indian Express. According to Farooq's letter, the ministers will be required to hold regular meetings with the advisory groups associated with them and keep its members informed about their policy initiatives and progress being made in their respective departments. Some NC legislators, when asked about Farooq's initiative, reacted cautiously, saying “Let's wait and see how things unfold’’. The proposed advisory groups may assuage the NC legislators' “bruised sentiments” to a degree as every MLA would have a say in matters concerning the ministers' policy decisions, party insiders said. “However, everything would depend on the mechanism and operation of these groups,’’ said a legislator. On October 27, Omar rejigged his ministry, taking it to a maximum of 9 members including the CM. This caused resentment among at least 18 MLAs who went into a huddle following the Cabinet reshuffle. In the 90-member J&K Assembly, the NC has 42 members. The party also has the support of six Congress MLAs and one CPI(M) member besides four Independent MLAs, which has increased the ruling coalition's tally to 53. With all eight ministers and Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather belonging to the NC, the party has 32 other MLAs. So, if four-member advisory groups are constituted and attached to each minister, the entire NC Legislature Party could be accommodated informally in the government's decision-making process, party leaders said. In July 1984, J&K saw an entire ruling legislature party accommodated in the ministry, when then dissident NC leader G M Shah toppled the Farooq Abdullah government to form his own government with 12 defector MLAs, which was then backed by the Congress. NC's play Meanwhile, in a bid to keep its flock together now, the NC leadership has also taken some additional initiatives to appease its legislators. It has formed a party disciplinary committee headed by a senior leader Khalid Najeeb Suharwardy with the party’s Kashmir and Jammu province presidents, Showkat Ahmad Mir and Rattan Lal Gupta, respectively, as its members. One of the NC MLAs, who was present at the November 6 meeting with Farooq, said they had also sought a change in a minister's portfolio besides the constitution of a manifesto review committee and strengthening of the party’s publicity cell. He claimed, “The dissenting MLAs only want the NC leadership to undertake reforms in the party to seize the opportunity arising out of growing public disenchantment with the BJP, especially in the Jammu region,” adding that they had become restive as they wanted “visible changes in the functioning of the party and the government”.

headline: 36 withdraw, 165 in fray for Patiala MC repolls
content: A total of 165 candidates are now in the electoral fray for the upcoming re-elections in 30 wards of the Patiala Municipal Corporation after 36 candidates withdrew their nomination papers on Saturday, according to the report received from the returning officers.A total of 201 nomination papers were found valid for the 30 wards after the scrutiny. However, 36 candidates withdrew their nominations, bringing the final number down to 165 candidates left in the fray.Interestingly, no candidate has been declared elected unopposed in any of the 30 wards. The report also indicates that the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) has not fielded any candidate in these elections.The elections are being held in 30 wards of the 60-ward Municipal Corporation of Patiala. The wards going to polls include Ward Numbers 1, 4, 6, 12, 14, 15, 16, 22, 26, 28, 32, 33, 34, 36, 37, 38, 40, 41, 43, 44, 45, 46, 48, 50, 51, 52, 53, 55, 57 and 58.With all four major political parties fielding candidates in every ward, the elections are expected to witness a multi-cornered contest, with Independent candidates also adding to the electoral challenge.

headline: BJP only alternative in Punjab: Ex-MLA Kamboj
content: Two-time former Rajpura MLA Hardyal Singh Kamboj today addressed a meeting with party workers and local leaders including Jaspal Singh. Local organisational leaders from Rajpura also participated in this meeting along with associates.Kamboj stated that neither the Congress nor the AAP party possesses any concrete programme to protect Punjab from issues such as drug abuse. He urged the general public to join the BJP, so that by forming a BJP government in Punjab, aligned with the BJP-led Central government, the issues facing the state could be resolved.Three days after joining the BJP, the meetings today were a show of strength by the leader, who is keen to contest the upcoming Vidhan Sabha polls. His joining the BJP is a major setback to the Congress ahead of the Punjab Assembly election.Kamboj has represented Rajpura in the Assembly and also served as the Congress’s in-charge for the constituency. His induction into the BJP adds to a series of defections to the saffron party in the recent week.Kamboj today said that the only alternative for Punjab at this crucial juncture is the BJP, which can do a lot for the youngsters and the people of Punjab. “With the AAP failing to control the menace of drugs and also the deteriorating law and order situation, people want a change”, he said.Talking to The Tribune, Kamboj, who is a seasoned legislator and has represented Rajpura in 2012 and 2017 by securing the second-highest victory margins for the Congress across Punjab on both occasions, said that the infighting in the Congress has helped no one and the people of the state feel ignored as leaders try to be front-runners for the CM post. “I am sure that the BJP will form the next government and the people of the state have also made up their mind to teach the AAP and the Congress a lesson”, he said.Earlier, Jaspal Singh also expressed his heartfelt gratitude to the workers who attended, assuring them that everyone who joins the BJP will be accorded due respect.Kamboj was inducted into the party at the BJP office in Chandigarh on Thursday in the presence of the Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Saini, who has been actively campaigning in Punjab as the BJP steps up its poll preparation. Hundreds of Kamboj supporters had also joined the saffron party.

headline: Rahul Gandhi breaks from Sonia, Priyanka on Israel. Left allies hit out
content: Senior Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s support for strong ties with Israel due to “strategic interests”, while condemning both the October 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas on civilians in Israel, and Israel’s war on Gaza since, is a moderation from the party’s stand and has drawn condemnation from its allies. While both Sonia Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra have used the word “genocide” while describing Israel’s actions in Gaza, Gandhi’s remarks – during an interaction at University of Chicago this week – are, in fact, closer to the position maintained by the Indian government led by Narendra Modi, which has sought to balance ties between Israel and the Arab world. In a sharp reaction on Saturday, former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan, whose party CPI(M) is a close ally of the Congress at the Centre, said Gandhi’s remarks “expose the Congress party’s glaring hypocrisy on Palestine”. “His pro-imperialist position undermines the legacy of Nehru, whose foreign policy stood firmly against imperialism and in solidarity with the Palestinian struggle,” Vijayan posted on X. Another ally, the CPI(ML) Liberation, called for an end to India’s relationship with Israel. Describing it as a "genocidal regime", CPI (ML) Liberation general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said there could be no strategic relationship with a State that continued to perpetrate genocide against "children, women and common people despite global condemnation". Gandhi’s call for strong ties with Israel is also striking because the Modi government has been criticised for its perceived closeness to Israel PM Benjamin Netanyahu, whose hawkish policy has driven the war on Gaza. Modi visited Israel just days before the US and Israel launched their attacks on Iran on February 28 this year. Gandhi shared his remarks on Israel, during a conversation with Professor Robert Pape at the University of Chicago, on X. The Congress leader said: “India’s foreign policy must be guided by what is good for India… I support a strong relationship with Israel. We have strategic interests, including buying the best weapons for our armed forces.” At the same time, this “cannot mean silence on Gaza”, Gandhi said. “I condemn the October 7th attacks and the killing of innocent people. I also condemn what Israel has done in Gaza. One wrong cannot justify another… We are a nation of 1.5 billion people. No country – Israel, USA, Russia or China – should hold us back from playing our rightful role on the global stage. India must stand for what it believes in.” Gandhi’s sister and senior Congress leader Vadra has been among the most critical voices in the party when it comes to Israel. On August 12, 2025, she accused the Israeli government of committing “genocide” and said it is “shameful” that the Indian government is standing “silent” on this. She has also worn Palestine tote bags as a symbol of her support. In June, in an op-ed in The Indian Express, Sonia Gandhi wrote: “The calculus of national interest demands that we respond to the global public opinion against the Israeli regime’s genocidal actions in Gaza and its brutal displacement and dispossession of lakhs of Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank. The Modi government’s continued silence simply cannot be explained rationally or morally.” In a response to Vadra’s remarks, Israeli Ambassador to India Reuven Azar had said: “What is shameful is your deceit. Israel killed 25,000 Hamas terrorists. The terrible cost in human lives derives from Hamas’s heinous tactics of hiding behind civilians, their shooting of people trying to evacuate or receive assistance and their rocket fire… Israel facilitated 2 million tonnes of food into Gaza while Hamas tries to sequester them, thereby creating hunger. Gaza population has grown 450 per cent in the last 50 years, no genocide there. Don’t buy Hamas numbers.” The Congress itself has treaded more carefully, with its historic support for Palestine requiring a modulation after the October 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas. The Congress initially refrained from naming Hamas and using the word “terror” to describe the attacks. But party leaders like Shashi Tharoor questioned this, seeking at a meeting of the Congress Working Committee (CWC) on October 9, 2023, that a resolution be passed condemning the attacks, naming the outfit and using the word terror. While the CWC ignored the suggestion, soon afterwards, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge condemned “the brutal attacks by Hamas on the people of Israel”, adding that “the indiscriminate actions by Israel’s military forces in civilian areas, that includes a siege of the Gaza Strip and bombings in it” were also “unacceptable”. Later, the Congress joined Left parties in slamming the Modi government after India abstained from voting at the UN General Assembly on a resolution drafted by Arab states calling for an immediate truce between Israel and Hamas and demanding aid access to the Gaza Strip. In his post Saturday criticising Rahul Gandhi, Vijayan said: “At a time when Gaza is witnessing one of the most devastating genocides of our time, with thousands of innocent children among its victims, he openly advocates stronger ties with Israel and arms purchases from a state responsible for their slaughter. His attempt to strike a diplomatic balancing act in the face of this catastrophe is indefensible… There can be no balancing act when humanity is on trial.” In a Facebook post, sharing a report on Gandhi's comments, CPI (ML) Liberation leader Bhattacharya said: “Just as there could be no strategic relationship with Nazi Germany or the apartheid state of South Africa, there can be no normalising, condoning or downplaying of the genocide in Gaza or the cruel colonial occupation of Palestine by Israel.” He added: “India's existing strategic relationship with Israel, the growing Adani-led corporate trade including arms supply, and sinister use of Israel’s surveillance technology and security model has already done enough damage to India's international image, foreign policy credibility and above all the health of our own internal democracy and governance. We must end it sooner rather than later and must not rationalise it in the name of India's defence or ‘national security’ needs.”

headline: Dry cold intensifies in Himachal; sub-zero temperatures in tribal areas
content: Shimla, Nov 22 (PTI) Dry cold has intensified in Himachal Pradesh, with night temperatures dropping below the freezing point in tribal areas and dense morning fog in the plains and river-valley regions. On Sunday, visibility in Sundernagar (Mandi district) plummeted to just 70 meters due to fog, causing difficulties for motorists. There is no likelihood of rain or snowfall in the state until November 28, the Met said. So far in November, the state received 3.1 mm of rain against normal rainfall of 12.2 mm, a deficit of 74 per cent from November 1 to 22. The lack of precipitation is exacerbating the dry cold conditions. The state’s average minimum temperature recorded a decline of 0.2 degrees Celsius over the last 24 hours. Tabo, in the Lahaul-Spiti district, was the coldest in the state, with a minimum temperature of -4.6 degrees Celsius. In Palampur, the temperature was 2 degrees Celsius below normal. In Nahan, it was 1.5 and in Bilaspur and Chamba, it was 0.5 and 0.3 degrees Celsius below normal, respectively. PTI BPL MNK This report is auto-generated from PTI news service. ThePrint holds no responsibility for its content.

headline: Criticise decisions, not constitutional institutions: CJI
content: Shimla, Nov 22 (PTI) Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant on Sunday said that citizens in a democracy have the right to criticise the decisions of constitutional bodies but should avoid targeting the institutions themselves. Interacting with students on the sidelines of the 10th convocation of the Central University of Himachal Pradesh (CUHP) at Dharamshala, where he was the chief guest, the Chief Justice observed that people often fail to distinguish between a decision and the institution behind it. According to him, this tendency risks undermining public confidence in institutions essential to sustaining democracy, a university statement said. While citizens in a democracy have the right to criticise the decisions of constitutional bodies, they should avoid targeting the institutions themselves, he said. In his convocation address on Sunday, Justice Surya Kant drew on the Himalayan landscape around him to urge the graduating students to be patient in pursuing their goals, reminding them that the road to any destination in the mountains is seldom straight and that no one climbs a mountain alone. The convocation was held at the auditorium of Government Degree College, Dharamshala. Degrees were conferred on 702 students and 32 gold medals were presented, 23 of them to women.

headline: Himachal eyes 500 MW solar capacity, pushes major hydropower projects
content: Shimla: Himachal Pradesh is accelerating its transition towards renewable energy, with the state government targeting the installation of 500 MW of solar power capacity while simultaneously expediting several major hydropower and pumped storage projects across the state. The Himachal Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (HPPCL) has generated 3,459.99 million units (MUs) of electricity and earned revenue of Rs 1,387.49 crore from its operational projects over the last four years since December 2022. The 100 MW Sainj Hydroelectric Project in Kullu district and the 11 MW Sawra Kuddu Hydroelectric Project in Shimla district have been among the major contributors. Sainj generated 1,252.56 MUs, earning Rs 462.55 crore, while Sawra Kuddu contributed 1,190.383 MUs and generated revenue of Rs 589.6 crore. Similarly, the 65 MW Kashang Stage-I Hydroelectric Project in Kinnaur generated 776.328 MUs of electricity, earning Rs 252 crore. Solar power projects have also contributed to the corporation’s growing renewable energy portfolio. The 32 MW Pekhubela project in Una district generated 113.27 MUs and earned Rs 32.89 crore. The project was inaugurated by Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu on June 20, 2024. Other commissioned solar projects include the 5 MW Berra Dol project in Bilaspur, which generated 62.78 MUs and earned Rs 27.05 crore, the 5 MW Bhanjal project in Una, which contributed 18.87 MUs and Rs 6.83 crore, and the 10 MW Aghlor project, which generated 25.02 MUs and earned Rs 7.75 crore.

headline: UPSC Key: Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, Fake Medical Licences and Climate Talks
content: Written by Sanju Singh Important topics and their relevance in UPSC CSE exam for November 22, 2026. If you missed the November 21, 2026 UPSC CSE exam key from the Indian Express, read it here. FRONT PAGE Shah: Siang dam national project, we will hold talks Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: Geography of India, Major rivers and river systems, Hydropower projects and dams in India, India’s strategic location; India-China relations. Mains Examination: GS Paper III- Infrastructure, Energy; environmental impact assessment; conservation and environmental concerns; disaster management. What’s the ongoing story: In his first public remarks on the proposed 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh, Union Home Minister Amit Shah described the project as a national project crucial to the state's development and offered talks and a comprehensive rehabilitation package to the affected communities. His remarks came amid protests by residents and indigenous communities who have consistently opposed the proposed project. Key Points to Ponder: — What is the strategic significance of the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project for India's energy security and its northeastern frontier? — Discuss the significance of hydropower projects in India's efforts to strengthen energy security. — Examine the environmental and socio-cultural concerns associated with large dam projects in ecologically fragile and tribal regions. — How can the government balance strategic infrastructure development with the rights and concerns of indigenous communities? — Discuss the geopolitical implications of China's hydropower projects on the Yarlung Tsangpo river for India. Key Takeaways: — The Siang Indigenous Farmers’ Forum (SIFF) and the Adi Bane Kebang United submitted a joint memorandum to Shah on November 20, seeking cancellation of the project, an immediate halt to pre-feasibility work and a judicial inquiry into the October 23 violence. — The affected communities, Shah said, would receive a comprehensive rehabilitation package. He also assured them that their heritage, culture and religious beliefs would be protected. — His remarks are significant because they reiterate the project’s strategic importance and reaffirm the Centre’s resolve to build the dam, while leaving the terms of consultation open. — Plans to harness the Siang and Subansiri date back to 1982. In 2017, NITI Aayog proposed replacing two planned upper Siang projects with one large storage dam. — In December 2024, Beijing approved a 60,000-MW project with five cascade power stations on the lower Yarlung Tsangpo, sharpening concerns in India over downstream flows and sudden releases of water. — The SIFF estimates that the reservoir could submerge 27 villages, affect dozens more and displace between one lakh and 1.5 lakh indigenous people. Do You Know? — The Siang is the upper course of the Brahmaputra. The river originates in the Tibetan Plateau, where it is known as the Yarlung Tsangpo. It flows eastwards through Tibet, makes a sharp horseshoe-shaped bend around the Namcha Barwa peak, and enters Arunachal Pradesh, where it is known as the Siang or Dihang. It subsequently flows into Assam, where the Siang, Dibang and Lohit river systems come together to form the Brahmaputra. —The Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) evolved from two separate hydropower projects. In 2017, the government proposed replacing the planned 5,500-MW Siang Upper Stage-I and 3,750-MW Siang Upper Stage-II projects with a single, larger multipurpose project. The preliminary report submitted by NHPC in December 2022 envisaged an 11,000-MW project with a reservoir capacity of 9 billion cubic metres. — The Siang basin has a complex Himalayan river geography. The Central Water Commission's basin assessment identifies six major river sub-basins in Arunachal Pradesh: Kameng, Subansiri, Siang (Dihang), Dibang, Lohit and Tirap. These rivers and their tributaries drain into the Brahmaputra river system. The Siang basin covers Upper Siang, West Siang and East Siang districts. (150 words) (UPSC CSE 2018, GS Paper 4) India, China meet again to try and calm Arunachal frontier Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: India-China boundary dispute, Important geographical features and international boundaries, Line of Actual Control (LAC) Mains Examination: GS Paper II- India and its neighbourhood relations; bilateral agreements involving India and affecting its interests. GS Paper III- security challenges and their management in border areas. What’s the ongoing story: India and China have concluded the second round of Corps Commander-level talks to resolve tensions along the frontier in Arunachal Pradesh before the onset of winter. The closely guarded talks began immediately after Diwali on November 8 and continued for nearly 10 days, with a short break in between. Lt General Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army’s III Corps, also called the Spear Corps, held talks with his Chinese counterpart and other officers. An official from the Ministry of External Affairs was also present. Key Points to Ponder: — What is the significance of Corps Commander-level talks in maintaining peace and tranquillity along the India-China border? — Explain the difference between the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and the McMahon Line. — Discuss the major challenges in managing India's border with China, particularly in the eastern sector. — Examine how differences in perceptions of the boundary and infrastructure development contribute to tensions along the LAC. Key Takeaways: — India and China have concluded the second round of Corps Commander-level talks to resolve tensions along the frontier in Arunachal Pradesh before winter sets in fully. The talks were held to set engagement rules between the two sides, avoid friction between troops on the ground, ensure open communication lines and bring down tensions before winter. — The III Corps, or Spear Corps, has its headquarters at Rangapahar near Dimapur in Nagaland. The first Corps Commander-level talks in the eastern sector were held on September 6–7, 2026, at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point. Wacha is India's easternmost border personnel meeting point, located in the Kibithoo sector. — In August, National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the special representatives for the boundary talks between the two countries, met in Beijing. — Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu said that transgressions continue along the frontier because China does not recognise the McMahon Line. — Former Chief of Defence Staff Lt Gen Anil Chauhan (retd) said that the unsettled boundary issue, differing perceptions of the boundary, infrastructure construction and force multipliers create the possibility of friction and escalation. He emphasised vigilance, credible capabilities, clear agreements and consistent adherence to them. Do You Know? — The India-China border is conventionally divided into the Western Sector (Ladakh), Middle Sector (Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand) and Eastern Sector (Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh). According to the Indian Express, the two countries have differing perceptions of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), which has historically resulted in face-offs between troops. — The Ministry of External Affairs has clarified that there is no commonly delineated LAC between India and China and that the two countries do not share a common perception of its entire alignment. Some areas have overlapping perceptions, which can lead to face-offs between patrols. — The McMahon Line forms the basis of the boundary alignment in the eastern sector: It was drawn by Sir Henry McMahon, the Foreign Secretary of British India, during the 1914 Simla Convention between British India, Tibet and China. The approximately 890-km line demarcated the boundary between British India and Tibet. China does not recognise this line. — The 1993 and 1996 agreements provide the framework for maintaining peace along the LAC: The 1993 Agreement on the Maintenance of Peace and Tranquillity along the LAC and the 1996 Agreement on Confidence-Building Measures in the Military Field seek to prevent escalation and maintain stability pending a final settlement of the boundary question. They include provisions concerning military-force levels and respect for the LAC. (UPSC CSE 2024, GS Paper 3) No voter-deletion forms for BJP workers in UP in this round of electoral roll preparation Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: Election Commission of India, Representation of the People Act, 1950, Electoral rolls and electoral registration. Mains Examination: GS Paper II: Salient features of the Representation of the People Act; appointment to various Constitutional posts, powers, functions and responsibilities of constitutional bodies; issues relating to the electoral process and electoral reforms. What’s the ongoing story: Amid complaints from several constituencies in Uttar Pradesh of bulk submission of Form 7 for deletion of names from electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), leading to FIRs in some cases, the BJP has decided not to provide Form 7 to its Booth Level Agents (BLAs) involved in the ongoing Special Summary Revision (SSR). As per sources, BJP workers are being given only Form 6 (for inclusion of names) and Form 8 (filed for shifting of residence/corrections). The party has therefore sent its BLAs lists of names deleted during the SIR under the categories of ‘absent, shifted, dead or duplicate’ for rechecking through door-to-door visits. Key Points to Ponder: — What is the role of the Election Commission of India in the preparation, revision and maintenance of electoral rolls? — Differentiate between Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and Special Summary Revision (SSR) of electoral rolls. — Explain the provisions of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, relating to the preparation and revision of electoral rolls. — What are the respective roles of Booth Level Officers (BLOs), Booth Level Agents (BLAs) and Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) in the electoral roll preparation process? — Examine how wrongful exclusion of eligible voters from electoral rolls can affect the principle of universal adult suffrage. Key Takeaways: — The development comes amid allegations of large-scale deletion of genuine voters during the SIR in Uttar Pradesh. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has claimed that 1.27 crore Hindu voters were deleted in the state, while Muslim voters had increased by 1.65%. — The Election Commission of India has also been facing scrutiny over allegations of bulk submission of Form 7 applications and voter deletions. The Supreme Court has been nudging the poll panel to allow voters left out of electoral rolls during the SIR to reapply. — The BJP has launched a month-long ‘Matdata Jodo Abhiyan’ to identify eligible voters whose names were left out of the electoral rolls and facilitate their inclusion. — The draft electoral rolls published following the SSR put the number of voters in Uttar Pradesh as of November 17 at 13.58 crore, which was 18.84 lakh more than the electoral rolls published on April 10 following the SIR. — “As part of the campaign, the BJP has provided workers in every Assembly seat around 5,000 copies of Form 6 and 1,000 copies of Form 8, along with a copy of the electoral roll and the list of deleted names. No Form 7 is being provided as the party wants to use its energy and human resources towards the inclusion of new and left-out voters.” Do You Know? — The Election Commission of India (ECI) is constitutionally responsible for the preparation of electoral rolls. Article 324 of the Constitution vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the ECI. — The preparation and revision of electoral rolls are governed by the Representation of the People Act (RPA), 1950, and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. Section 21 of the RPA, 1950 empowers the ECI to direct the preparation and revision of electoral rolls, including special revisions. — Under Rule 25 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, electoral roll revision may be conducted intensively, summarily or partly through both methods. In an intensive revision, the electoral roll is prepared afresh, whereas in a summary revision, the existing electoral roll is updated through additions, deletions and corrections. — Following the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, the qualifying dates for determining eligibility for registration as an elector are January 1, April 1, July 1 and October 1 of the year. An Indian citizen who has attained or will attain 18 years of age on any of these dates can apply for registration. — Section 22 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, provides for correction, transposition and deletion of entries in electoral rolls. Entries may be deleted on grounds such as death, a person ceasing to be ordinarily resident in the constituency or being otherwise not entitled to registration. The provision also requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard in specified circumstances before deletion. Discuss the position of the Election Commission of India while undertaking the revision of electoral rolls. Can it also examine the question of citizenship of voters? (UPSC CSE 2026, GS Paper 2) NATION Real doctors, fake licences Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: National Medical Commission (NMC); Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE); regulation of medical practitioners; medical education in India. Mains Examination: GS II- Statutory and regulatory bodies; issues relating to the development and management of the health sector; government policies and interventions. GS IV-Probity in governance; transparency and ethical conduct in public services. What’s the ongoing story: In Buldhana, a district in eastern Maharashtra, Sanket Unhale, 26, had been seeing patients since August, police say, working alongside his uncle, a doctor at a local hospital. Varun Akhade, 28, from the same district, was practising on his own. Both had studied medicine in the Philippines, and both held certificates from the Maharashtra Medical Council (MMC), the body that registers doctors in the state, saying they were cleared to practise in India. These entries, which belonged to 22 applicants, were of people recorded as having studied medicine abroad and cleared the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE), the screening test conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), that a foreign-trained medical graduate must pass before practising in India. Key Points to Ponder: — What is the role of the National Medical Commission and State Medical Councils in regulating medical practitioners? — Why is the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination mandatory for foreign-trained medical graduates seeking to practise in India? — What are the institutional and technological safeguards required to protect medical registration databases? — How can fraudulent medical registration affect patient safety and public trust in healthcare? — What challenges do high medical education costs and limited availability of medical seats pose for aspiring doctors? Key Takeaways: — Maharashtra Medical Council's (MMC) database was allegedly compromised before its June 2026 security upgrade, enabling unauthorised access and manipulation of records. — None of the 22 applicants had actually cleared the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE), despite their records showing otherwise. Forged certificates were allegedly issued to them. — Foreign medical graduates ordinarily undergo a verification process, including confirmation of their qualifications directly from the overseas university, which usually takes around three months. One accused allegedly charged ₹15–25 lakh per applicant for facilitating fake clearances. — Over 20 lakh candidates compete for around 1.4 lakh MBBS seats in India in 2026, while FMGE pass rates have remained low—just over 18% in 2026. — MMC is seeking an additional security audit by a Government of India-recognised company to prevent further breaches. Do You Know: — The Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) is a mandatory screening test for Indian citizens and Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) who obtain their primary medical qualifications abroad and seek registration to practise allopathic medicine in India. Foreign medical graduates must qualify the examination to obtain provisional or permanent registration with the National Medical Commission (NMC) or a State Medical Council. The examination is conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS). — In November 2023, the NMC clarified that foreign medical graduates would have to appear for the screening test, or the National Exit Test (NExT) that was proposed to replace it, within 10 years of completing their course. It also specified that the entire course, training and internship must be completed at the same university. — The clarification addressed difficulties faced by students whose education was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine war. For certain students who had completed their education under earlier arrangements, the NMC prescribed additional clinical clerkship and internship requirements to address deficiencies in training. (UPSC CSE 2024, GS Paper 2) Kashmir now has no local militants, but the threat is far from over Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: Jammu and Kashmir; Line of Control (LoC); terrorism and security-related organisations; internal security mechanisms. Mains Examination: GS III- Linkages between development and spread of extremism; role of external state and non-state actors in creating challenges to internal security. What’s the ongoing story: The killing of Mohammad Lateef Bhat in a gunfight in South Kashmir’s Kulgam on Wednesday marked an unprecedented moment in Kashmir — for the first time since the onset of militancy in 1989, there was no local terrorist active in the Valley. But for security forces, the challenge in Kashmir has been severely curtailed many times in the past, it has rebounded too. Security officials believe the absence of local terrorists could also diminish the operational capabilities of Lashkar’s foreign operatives. While the local terror network in the Valley is believed to have been wiped out, Jammu has at least three active local terrorists — all of them from Kishtwar — including Mohammad Amin alias Jahangir Saroori. Key Points to Ponder: — How has the nature of militancy in Jammu and Kashmir evolved since 1989? — How do foreign terrorist operatives influence the security situation in Jammu and Kashmir? — What are the geographical and operational challenges posed by the Pir Panjal range for security forces? — How can intelligence-led operations, border management and community engagement help prevent the revival of local militancy? — What is the significance of the decline in local recruitment for India's internal security? Key Takeaways: — Militancy in Kashmir has been curtailed on several occasions in the past, only to return later. In 2013, for instance, the number of active terrorists in the Valley had fallen below 80, with fewer than 35 local terrorists. South Kashmir, which later became an epicentre of militancy under Burhan Wani, had witnessed a particularly sharp decline. — Despite the absence of local terrorists in the Valley, police sources estimate that around 30 LeT operatives remain active there, most of them in mountainous forest areas. Security officials believe that the lack of local recruits and support could make it more difficult for these foreign operatives to plan and execute major attacks. — According to the article, several major LeT attacks in the past were possible because of local support. The weakening of local networks could therefore restrict the ability of foreign terrorists to carry out large-scale operations. — While the local terror network in the Valley is believed to have been wiped out, Jammu continues to have at least three active local terrorists, all from Kishtwar. One of them is Mohammad Amin, also known as Jahangir Saroori. — Foreign LeT operatives have carried out almost all major attacks on security forces on both sides of the Pir Panjal mountains and in mainland Jammu. Tackling these operatives remains a major security challenge. Do You Know: — According to data provided by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) in the Rajya Sabha on February 7, 2024, the number of terrorist-initiated incidents in Jammu and Kashmir declined from 153 in 2019 to 46 in 2023. The number of encounters and counter-terrorism operations also fell from 102 in 2019 to 48 in 2023. The number of terrorists killed declined from 157 in 2019 to 73 in 2023. — The MHA's Annual Report 2024–25 identifies cross-border terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir as an internal security concern. It also highlights the role of capacity-building of State Police Forces in intelligence collection, response to terrorist incidents and subsequent investigations. The report notes that terrorist organisations and individuals involved in terrorist activities are listed under the First and Fourth Schedules, respectively, of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967. Discuss the measures adopted by the Government in this respect as part of conflict resolution in Jammu and Kashmir.”(UPSC CSE 2023, GS Paper 3) OPINION Before COPs: The turning point in climate talks Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Conference of the Parties (COP), Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC). Mains Examination: GS III- Environmental pollution and degradation; conservation; climate change; international environmental conventions and agreements. What’s the ongoing story: Amitabh Sinha writes that the history of international climate negotiations is often traced to the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, but the process of building a global climate framework began much earlier. Scientific discussions on rising carbon dioxide concentrations and global warming had already gained momentum in the 1970s and 1980s. The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) organised a climate conference in Geneva in 1979. In October 1985, the WMO and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) convened a conference in Villach, Austria. The meeting assessed the combined influence of major greenhouse gases on the climate and projected a possible global temperature rise of 1.5–4.5°C by the 2030s. Key Points to Ponder: — Why should the origins of international climate negotiations be traced to the scientific discussions of the 1970s and 1980s rather than only to the 1992 Rio Earth Summit? — Examine the contribution of the Villach Conference of 1985 to the development of global climate governance. — How did the establishment of the UNFCCC institutionalise international cooperation on climate change? — Explain the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC). Why is it important for developing countries such as India? — Examine the role of the Conference of the Parties (COP) under Article 7 of the UNFCCC in shaping global climate agreements. Key Takeaways: Amitabh Sinha writes: — “The Villach Conference of 1985 was a turning point. Organised jointly by the WMO and UNEP, it assessed the combined influence of major greenhouse gases on the global climate. It projected a possible temperature rise of 1.5–4.5°C by the 2030s and recommended continuous scientific assessment of greenhouse gas concentrations and their consequences.” — “An advisory group on greenhouse gases was established in 1986. In 1988, it evolved into the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), following the decision of the WMO and UNEP to establish a more formal scientific body with governments involved.” — “Published in 1990, the IPCC's first Assessment Report highlighted the role of human activities in increasing greenhouse gas concentrations. This brought climate change more firmly into the international policy agenda. — “The UNFCCC recognised that developed countries, particularly members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), were primarily responsible for the increase in greenhouse gas concentrations and would have to bear the greater burden of addressing climate change.” — “The principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities recognises that countries have shared responsibility for addressing climate change, but their historical contributions and capacities to respond differ. Developing countries continue to invoke this principle in international climate negotiations.” — “Article 7 of the UNFCCC established the Conference of the Parties (COP), which meets annually to review the implementation of the Convention and any subsequent legal instruments. The COP process has provided the institutional platform for international climate negotiations.” Do You Know: — The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was adopted in May 1992 and opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in June 1992. It entered into force on March 21, 1994. The first Conference of the Parties (COP 1) was held in Berlin in 1995. — Adopted at COP 3 in Kyoto, Japan, on December 11, 1997, the Protocol operationalised the UNFCCC by setting binding greenhouse gas emission-reduction targets for industrialised countries and economies in transition. It entered into force on February 16, 2005. Its mechanisms included International Emissions Trading, the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) and Joint Implementation. — The Paris Agreement marked a shift towards a collective climate-action framework: Adopted at COP 21 on December 12, 2015, and brought into force on November 4, 2016, the Paris Agreement seeks to limit the rise in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Unlike the Kyoto Protocol's binding targets for developed countries, the Paris Agreement requires all Parties to prepare and communicate Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), reflecting their climate-action commitments. — Nationally Determined Contributions operate through a five-year cycle: Under the Paris Agreement, countries submit NDCs outlining their planned actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and strengthen adaptation. Each successive NDC is expected to represent progression beyond the previous one and reflect the country's highest possible ambition. The Agreement also provides for a Global Stocktake to assess collective progress towards its long-term goals. Statement II: Article 6 of the Paris Agreement on climate change sets out the principles of carbon markets. Statement III: Article 6 of the Paris Agreement on climate change intends to promote inter-country non-market strategies to reach their climate targets. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I (b) Both Statement II and Statement III are correct but only one of them explains Statement I (c) Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I (d) Neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct (6) “Describe the major outcomes of the 26th session of the Conference of the Parties (COP) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). What are the commitments made by India in this conference?”(UPSC CSE 2021, GS Paper 3) ECONOMY Battery black mass export ban: A push for domestic recycling Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: Critical minerals and their applications, Battery recycling, e-waste management and circular economy, National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM) Mains Examination: GS III-Indian Economy and issues relating to planning, mobilisation of resources, growth and development; infrastructure; environmental pollution and degradation; conservation; e-waste management; indigenisation of technology. What’s the ongoing story: The Centre, on November 10, 2026, prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass and related battery waste with immediate effect. The decision came a day after China extended its restrictions on critical mineral exports for two months amid trade tensions involving the US and Europe. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, amended the export policy of lithium-ion battery black mass under ITC (HS) Code 85491400 from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’ through Notification No. 49 Key Points to Ponder: — What is black mass, and why is it considered an important secondary source of critical minerals? — How can battery recycling reduce India's dependence on imports of critical minerals? — Examine the significance of the DGFT's decision to prohibit black mass exports for India's domestic battery recycling industry. What are the challenges in developing an integrated domestic battery recycling and critical mineral refining ecosystem? Discuss the relationship between critical mineral security, electric mobility and India's clean energy transition. How does the recycling of lithium-ion batteries contribute to the circular economy and the concept of urban mining? Examine the significance of the National Critical Mineral Mission in strengthening India's critical mineral supply chains. Key Takeaways: — India has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass with effect from November 10, 2026, to ensure that battery waste generated domestically is processed and refined within the country. — Black mass is the powder-like material obtained after waste lithium-ion batteries and consumer electronics are broken down. It contains lithium, cobalt, manganese, nickel, silicon, tin, rhenium and graphite, which can be recovered and reused in battery manufacturing. — India has limited domestic reserves of several critical minerals and remains heavily dependent on imports. China controls around 90% of global critical mineral processing, leaving Indian industries vulnerable to supply disruptions. — India generates approximately 50,000 tonnes of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries annually. Industry estimates suggest that around 50% of this material, or 25,000 tonnes, can be converted into black mass. — In January 2025, the Technical Review Committee of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change classified black mass as hazardous waste unless it is processed on the same premises for the recovery of critical minerals. Its import and export are regulated under the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016. — The restriction could affect domestic recycling companies differently. Those that only dismantle batteries and produce black mass may face restrictions on their international market, while companies capable of extracting and refining metals into usable compounds could benefit from assured domestic feedstock. — The government expects the restriction to improve feedstock availability for domestic recycling and refining units, increase capacity utilisation, encourage investment and generate employment. — The larger objective is to retain critical minerals within India, promote domestic value addition, reduce import dependence and strengthen the country's battery recycling and refining ecosystem. Do You Know: — Lithium-ion battery recycling involves mechanical and chemical processes. According to NITI Aayog, mechanical processing includes collecting, sorting, discharging, dismantling and crushing used batteries to produce black mass. Hydrometallurgical processing then uses leaching, purification and crystallisation to recover metals as salts. Pyrometallurgy is another method of metal recovery. — In January 2025, the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) issued an SOP for utilising black mass generated from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries. It provides for recovering graphite and metals such as cobalt, manganese, nickel, lithium, copper, iron, aluminium and sodium, along with requirements for facilities, authorisation and regulatory compliance. — In January 2025, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change considered black mass under the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016. The Technical Review Committee held that black mass processed on the same premises for critical mineral recovery could be treated as an intermediate product. However, if transported or sold to another processing unit, it is treated as hazardous waste under the applicable rules. Cobalt 2. Graphite 3. Lithium 4. Nickel How many of the above usually make up battery cathodes? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) Only three (d) All the four India, Canada conclude sixth round of talks for proposed trade pact Syllabus: Preliminary Examination: India’s trade relations with Canada. Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements (CEPA) and Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreements (CECA). Mains Examination: GS II- Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and affecting India's interests. GS III- effects of liberalisation on the economy; changes in industrial policy and their effects on industrial growth. What’s the ongoing story: India and Canada have concluded the sixth round of negotiations for a proposed Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), with both countries aiming to finalise the agreement by the end of 2026. The 10-day round was held in New Delhi from November 11 to 20, 2026. Discussions covered key areas such as trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, trade remedies, intellectual property and investment promotion. Key Points to Ponder: — What is a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), and how does it differ from a Free Trade Agreement (FTA)? — What are the key components of a trade agreement, including trade in goods and services, rules of origin, trade remedies and intellectual property rights? — What opportunities could the India–Canada CEPA create for trade, investment, farmers, industries and MSMEs? — What challenges have affected India–Canada economic relations, and how could the proposed CEPA contribute to their revival? Key Takeaways: — The negotiations have a long history. The first attempt to negotiate a CEPA was launched in 2010 but failed to make substantial progress. Talks were relaunched in 2022 but suspended in 2023 following a deterioration in bilateral political relations. In March 2026, both countries decided to restart formal negotiations. — Discussions focused on trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, trade remedies, intellectual property and investment promotion. These areas will determine the extent of market access and the commercial benefits available to businesses in both countries. — Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to an agreement that would deliver tangible benefits to farmers, industries, businesses and micro, small and medium enterprises. — The proposed CEPA is expected to create new trade and investment opportunities, strengthen resilient and diversified supply chains, and deepen economic ties between India and Canada. Do You Know? — A Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) is a broad economic agreement covering trade in goods and services, investment and intellectual property rights. It can also address regulatory barriers and improve market access for services. — A Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) reduces tariffs on selected products, while a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) seeks to eliminate or substantially reduce tariffs on a wider range of goods. Both countries retain their own tariff policies for non-member countries.- — India–Canada economic relations: — According to the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, bilateral trade stood at US$8.66 billion in 2024–25. — India's major exports to Canada include pharmaceuticals, iron and steel, seafood, cotton garments, electronic goods and chemicals. Imports include pulses, coal, fertilisers, paper and crude petroleum. — Energy, critical minerals, agri-food, digital and clean technologies, education and services are potential areas for deeper economic cooperation. — In March 2026, India and Canada also signed a Memorandum of Understanding on critical minerals cooperation, covering exploration, mining, beneficiation and processing. This supports India's efforts to diversify supplies of minerals required for batteries, clean energy and advanced manufacturing. headline: India-China military discussions, on for over 2 months, end for now
content: Military officials from India and China have concluded a discussion — over the past few weeks — in the eastern sector of the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border, for the time being, according to sources. The talks started on September 6-7, ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s September 12-13 New Delhi visit for the Brics summit. While there’s little specific information on the military discussion, it was called to ease tensions at the border near Arunachal Pradesh, where locals spotted Chinese troops and graffiti since July. In October, a then-top official of a paramilitary force also publicly confirmed that many “faceoffs” had happened. The latest corps commander-level talks were led by Lt Gen Girish Kalia, commander of the Indian Army’s III Corps, and a senior People’s Liberation Army officer, likely from its Western Theater Command, as was the case in early September. A source said on Sunday that “de-escalation was visible” on the ground there. A foreign policy analyst recently told Business Standard that the situation was “under control” amid “heavy deployment” of Indian troops. And, India “has a military advantage” in that terrain today, especially after the lessons learnt from the 1962 war. The last round of India-China boundary talks between special representatives National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing in August prompted the first corps commander-level talks in this sector. India and China do not agree on the length of their border and have different perceptions of claim lines. The eastern sector spans Sikkim to Arunachal; the least contentious middle sector stretches along Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand in India, and Tibet in China. The western sector runs along Ladakh and Chinese-controlled Aksai Chin, which India claims, making this the most militarised zone of the India-China border dispute. Since the Sino-Indian war, China has claimed Arunachal Pradesh. This year, the government standardised the names of 27 locations and natural features in Arunachal to counter Chinese cartographic campaigns of “renaming” places elsewhere. China is building what it calls the world’s largest hydropower station on a river in Tibet that is upstream from Arunachal. India has announced a large dam of its own in the state.

headline: NGT halts mining in Solan’s Kundlu Khad over illegal mechanised extraction | Hindustan Times
content: Taking strict note of environmental violations, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) has directed the Himachal Pradesh authorities to ensure no illegal mining takes place in the Kundlu Khad area of Nalagarh in Solan district.The order follows the final report of a tribunal-appointed joint committee, which found evidence of mechanised riverbed mining despite permissions allowing only manual extraction. The panel also recommended suspending all mining leases in the area until plans and clearances are reassessed and revised.Observing that effective measures are required to curb illegal operations, the NGT ordered authorities to prevent any unauthorised mining by the project proponents or others until the next hearing on February 1, 2027.In December 2025, Bagga Ram and other local villagers moved the NGT, alleging that illegal and excessive sand mining in Kundlu Khad—a tributary of the Sutlej river—had destroyed roughly 40 bighas of agricultural land and damaged nearby houses.Acting on the petition, the tribunal on April 2, 2026, constituted a joint committee comprising the Solan deputy commissioner and officials from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change (MoEFCC).Key violationsThe panel examined allegations of excessive sand, stone, and bajri extraction, heavy machinery use, and breaches of approved mining plans across three leases operating in Kundlu Khad: Jai Mata Stone Crusher, Nalagarh Stone Crusher, and RP Enterprises and Ruhani Stone Crusher. Its inspection revealed the following:Use of heavy machinery: Approved plans restricted operators to manual extraction without blasting, capping pit depth at one metre. However, inspections found excavation deeper than one metre at multiple sites. Geo-tagged photographs from complainants and satellite imagery reviewed by the panel confirmed the deployment of JCB machines on the riverbed.Breach of national guidelines: Operators failed to comply with the Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines, 2016. Violations included failing to maintain a buffer of three metres (or 10% of the river width, whichever is less) from the riverbank, and failing to demarcate lease boundaries with pillars and geo-referencing prior to starting operations.Unsustainable extraction limits: The panel flagged a massive mismatch between permitted extraction and natural replenishment. While the 2018 District Survey Report (DSR) assessed Kundlu Khad’s annual replenishment capacity at just 27,027 metric tonnes, the three leaseholders were collectively permitted to extract approximately 38,70,900 metric tonnes over five years—a figure that far exceeded the stream’s capacity and had already been exhausted.Based on these findings, the joint committee recommended that the state geologist and the State Level Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA), Himachal Pradesh, reassess and revise all existing mining plans and environmental clearances in line with the 2024 DSR.

headline: 'Assam aims Rs 4,000-crore skill push to become eastern India's skill capital': CM Himanta Biswa
content: Assam is targeting the status of eastern India's skill capital, with the state planning to invest over Rs 4,000 crore to upgrade ITIs and other skill-training institutions into world-class centres of excellence, ready to power a Viksit Bharat and an Atmanirbhar Assam, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said.Emphasising the importance of vocational training alongside higher education, Sarma said India's future depended not just on academic degrees but also on a skilled workforce.He referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's address at the platinum jubilee celebrations of IIT-Kharagpur and the fifth 'Kaushal Deekshant Samaroh' for ITI toppers in Lucknow, both held on Saturday."His message was clear: a Viksit Bharat will not be built by degrees alone, but by skilled hands, and ITI graduates deserve the same respect and stature as IIT alumni," Sarma said."Whether it is an IIT or an ITI, for me, both are equally the treasures of my country, the strength of my nation, and the future of India," he added.A key component of the initiative is an investment of over Rs 2,390 crore in collaboration with Tata Technologies and more than 20 global original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to upgrade 77 technical institutions, including 43 ITIs and 34 polytechnics, he added.Sarma said students at these institutions are being trained in emerging fields such as electric vehicles, industrial robotics, 3D printing, the Internet of Things and AI-driven manufacturing.The state is also setting up the Assam Skill University at Mangaldai with an investment of Rs 1,016 crore.It will be the first government skill university of its kind in eastern India, he claimed.The university will offer courses ranging from vocational diplomas to BTech, MBA and PhD programmes in areas such as artificial intelligence, data science and digital manufacturing, bridging the gap between vocational training and higher education, he said..Guwahati Diary | Tinsukia's biggest pvt investment in 15 years.Sarma also cited a Rs 600-crore 'Hub-and-Spoke School Skill Network', being implemented in partnership with Tata Nelco and the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan.The initiative will establish 50 skill hubs and 500 spoke centres across educational institutions through satellite connectivity, taking industry-oriented training to rural areas."The government is setting up industry-led ITI clusters and global mobility centres in Jorhat, in partnership with Numaligarh Refinery Ltd, and Tinsukia, with Oil India Ltd, to align training with the industrial requirements of the Northeast," he said.A Skill India International Centre is also coming up in Guwahati, along with nine multi-skill centres of excellence in districts including Majuli, Kokrajhar, Silchar and Dibrugarh.An international partnership with ITE Singapore will help prepare the state's youth for global employment opportunities, Sarma added."Our aspiration is clear -- Assam should not merely supply manpower to the rest of the country but emerge as the skill capital of eastern India, ready to power a Viksit Bharat and an Atmanirbhar Assam," he said.(With inputs from PTI).Follow The New headline: South Korea Education Minister Quits Amid AI Cheating Fears
content: South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin stepped down on Sunday after President Lee Jae Myung accepted his offer to resign over confusion caused by last-minute rule changes aimed at preventing cheating with artificial intelligence (AI) ahead of last week's national college entrance exam. Choi said various changes made just before the Suneung caused inconvenience to the public, including test takers. Suneung is the Korean abbreviation for the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), the country's annual college entrance exam, which was held last Thursday. "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," he said in a statement released by the ministry. "Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation." Lee accepted Choi's resignation about an hour after the minister announced his intention to step down, Cheong Wa Dae spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said in a notice to the press, Yonhap News Agency reported. Kang said the nomination process for Choi's successor will proceed in accordance with due procedures. The education ministry has come under fire for hastily announcing new anti-AI cheating rules right up until the eve of the test, causing widespread confusion among test takers and teachers.

headline: Sixth cave-in at Haryana Orbital Rail Tunnel damages homes in Nuh’s Sahsola
content: CHANDIGARH: A major cave-in occurred for the sixth time today in little over a month at an under-construction tunnel of Haryana Orbital Rail Corridor (HORC), damaging homes in Sahsola gram panchayat of Nuh district of Haryana as several houses developed wide cracks, forcing many villagers to sleep in the open. The villagers heard a loud, blast-like sound early in the morning thus they rushed out of their houses and they noticed deep pits in the fields near their houses. A house, a village link road stretching about 200 feet and a stretch of land measuring more than 400 feet sank. The subsidence crossed the barricades put up by the administration and reached the first row of houses. Thus many locals locked their houses and left for safer places as they feared a bigger disaster. While some have put up makeshift huts, while others have rented rooms to accommodate themselves and their cattle. Also several trees had been damaged and they demanded that the Forest Department assess the loss. The villagers alleged negligence, saying no concrete safety measures had been taken and added that the land acquisition was progressing slowly and they had received no firm assurance from the authorities. Unlike the October 10 collapse, the gas pipeline was not damaged this time. A Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL) pipeline running from Jamnagar to Loni in Ghaziabad was exposed as the soil gave way last time, but no leakage was reported. No injuries were reported. The Orbital Rail Corridor cave-ins began in early October, when the soil sank over the tunnel in Patuka, part of Sahsola. Villagers submitted a written complaint to the Nuh Deputy Commissioner on October 5, seeking a halt to the work. On October 10, a larger collapse damaged a government school building and a house and caused more than 500 metres of land to sink. It also exposed a GAIL gas pipeline. Further collapses followed on October 30 and November 4, when a government road caved in. Railway officials filled the road with soil, but it sank again on November 18. .An expert committee has been formed to investigate the issue but has not announced any findings.Urging farmers not to worry, a senior official of the Haryana Rail Corporation said that the repeated collapses had disturbed the underground balance at the site and a technical inquiry was going on. He added that the work had been stopped and the tunnel’s starting point had been backfilled."The houses in the affected area have been inspected and marked, and land acquisition has begun. Further tunnel construction will be planned only after the acquisition is complete, based on a new design and the expert committee’s report," he added.The 4.69-km twin tunnel is a major component of the 126-km HORC line, which is designed to carry double-stack container trains through the Aravalli foothills.Around 1.1 km of the tunnel is being cut through Aravalli rock and about 3.6 km through soil. Each tube will be 30 feet high and 30 feet wide and designed for passenger trains travelling at up to 160 km per hour and freight trains at 100 km per hour.Roughly Rs 1,200 crore of the corridor’s total cost has been earmarked for the tunnel. The project cost was originally pegged at Rs 5,618 crore but was revised to Rs 11,709 crore by officials earlier this year. Technical briefs have previously highlighted the risks of drilling in the terrain because of "low cover or overburden", non-cohesive soil and heavily fractured rock strata..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest
